summary: Started the ai-retry repo: package skeleton, tsdown build, Vitest config and a first retryable-error classifier, with 6 passing tests against a mocked model.
body:
Created the repo and set up the package with TypeScript in strict mode, tsdown for the ESM and CJS build, and Vitest. The entry point is src/index.ts and it exports nothing useful yet. The first real piece is src/is-retryable.ts, which decides whether an error from a model call is worth another attempt.

The classifier looks at the AI SDK APICallError first. It trusts the isRetryable flag the SDK already sets, which covers 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses. On top of that it treats network-level failures such as ECONNRESET and fetch failed as retryable, and a plain TypeError from a bad argument as not retryable.

For tests I wrote a small mock model in test/helpers/mock-model.ts. It implements the language model interface and takes a list of results or errors to return in order. This made it easy to assert how many times doGenerate was called. Six tests pass: a 429 is retryable, a 500 is retryable, a 400 is not, a network reset is, an unknown error is not, and a non-Error throw is not.

The build produces dist with type declarations, and I checked that a throwaway project can import the package. Nothing is wired to a retry loop yet. Next is the loop itself with a fixed delay, then backoff with jitter. I also still need to decide whether the API wraps a model or is a middleware. Leaning toward wrapping the model, since the AI SDK wraps models in the same way for its own middleware.

summary: Wrote the retry loop for doGenerate with a max attempts option; it stops on the first non-retryable error and rethrows the last error after the limit.
body:
Added src/retry-model.ts, which takes a language model and returns a new model whose doGenerate runs inside a loop. The loop calls the underlying model, and on an error asks is-retryable whether to go on. If the error is not retryable it is rethrown at once. If attempts run out, the last error is rethrown unchanged.

I first thought about throwing a new RetryError that holds all the errors. The AI SDK already has RetryError for its own built-in retries, and mixing the two would confuse people. For now I keep the last error as is and put an attempts count in a property on a wrapper only when needed. I left this as an open point.

The option is maxAttempts and it defaults to 3, counting the first call. An early version used maxRetries, and I renamed it after seeing that it was ambiguous: 3 retries or 3 calls. The tests cover success on the first call, success on the third, exhaustion after 3 calls with the last error shown, and a non-retryable error that gives exactly 1 call.

The delay is zero in tests via a fake sleep. Streaming is not handled yet; doStream just passes through. All 11 tests pass. Next is the delay between attempts.

summary: Added exponential backoff with full jitter between attempts, using an injectable random source so the delay tests are deterministic and need no real sleeping.
body:
The retry loop from the previous day retried immediately, which is useless against a rate limit. I added a backoff module with a base delay, a multiplier and a max delay cap. The delay for attempt n is a random value between zero and min(cap, base * multiplier^n), which is the full jitter variant. I chose it because it spreads out clients that fail at the same moment better than a fixed or equal jitter delay.

The random function and the sleep function are both injectable through an internal options object. Tests pass a fake random that returns fixed values and a sleep that records the requested delay, so nothing waits. Vitest fake timers were my first try, but they interacted badly with the promise chain and made two tests flaky, so I dropped them. Defaults are a 500 ms base, a factor of 2 and a 30 s cap. Eight new tests cover the growth, the cap and a random value of zero, and all 14 tests pass. Next I want to make the delays configurable in the public options and add a fallback to another model.

summary: Made the backoff settings public options with validation, so a negative delay or a factor below 1 now throws a clear error when the model is wrapped, not mid-call.
body:
Yesterday's backoff module had hard-coded defaults, so I exposed baseDelay, maxDelay and factor in the public options. Each one is validated when the model is created. A negative number, NaN, or a factor below 1 throws a TypeError naming the option, for example 'ai-retry: factor must be a number >= 1'. Failing early seemed better than a confusing sleep value in the middle of a request.

I also added a jitter option that accepts false for tests and for users who want fixed delays. With jitter off, the delay is exactly the capped exponential value. Six more tests cover the validation and the jitter switch, and the suite now has 20 passing tests. The typecheck caught that the option type allowed undefined for factor, which I fixed with a default merge step. The fallback to another model is next.

summary: Implemented the fallback chain for doGenerate, with per-model options, and found the attempt counter was shared across models, which would have starved the fallbacks.
body:
Built src/create-retryable.ts, which takes a model and an options object with a fallbacks array, and returns a model that runs the chain. Each entry is either a model or an object with a model and its own retry options.

The first version looked fine and passed 5 of 6 new tests. The failing one had a primary with maxAttempts 2 and a fallback with maxAttempts 3. The fallback made only 1 call. The cause was that the attempt counter lived in the outer function and was never reset when moving to the next model. So the fallback inherited the primary's count and ran out early.

The fix was to give each model its own loop invocation with a fresh counter, and to make the outer function only iterate over the list. That also made the code simpler. The retry loop is now a pure function from a model and options to a result, and the chain is a for loop that calls it.

I also added the rule about which errors fall through. When the primary throws a non-retryable error, the chain stops and rethrows. When it throws a retryable error and attempts run out, the chain moves on. If all models are exhausted, the error of the last model is thrown.

One detail came up while testing. The error thrown after the whole chain fails is the last one, but users will want to know what the earlier models did. I added an errors array as a property on a small wrapper only in the all-exhausted case, and I want to check if this is useful before keeping it.

The tests now cover: primary succeeds, primary fails then fallback succeeds, both fail, per-model attempts, and non-retryable stop. 24 tests pass. Streams still bypass all this and will need their own step.

summary: Exported the public types and wrote a first README with install, a basic example, fallback and the options table.
body:
Cleaned up the exports in src/index.ts so that only the factory function and the option types are public. The internal helpers stay unexported. I added RetryableOptions, BackoffOptions and FallbackEntry as named types, since users will want to build option objects outside the call.

To check the types I wrote a type test file with expectTypeOf from Vitest. It makes sure that a model passed in keeps its type, that a fallback entry accepts both a bare model and an object, and that an unknown option name is a compile error. One failure showed up: the options type was too loose and accepted a string for maxAttempts through an index signature I had left in by mistake. I removed it.

The README has an install line, a ten-line example with an OpenAI model falling back to an Anthropic one, and a table of options with defaults. I ran the example against mocks to make sure the code compiles.

I checked the package output with npm pack and looked at the file list. It contains dist and the README and the license only. The types field points to the right declaration file for both module formats. Left for next time: set up GitHub Actions and changesets.

summary: Set up GitHub Actions for lint, typecheck and tests on Node 20 and 22, and initialized changesets for versioning.
body:
Added .github/workflows/ci.yml that runs on pushes and pull requests. It installs with a frozen lockfile, runs the typecheck, the tests and the build. A matrix covers Node 20 and Node 22. The first run failed on Node 20 because a test used structuredClone differently than expected; the cause was that I relied on a fake timer behavior that differs between versions. I rewrote the test to use the injectable sleep instead of fake timers, which is more robust anyway.

Next I ran changeset init and set the access to public and the base branch to main. A changeset file describes the first release as a minor bump from 0.0.0, and I wrote its text by hand. The release workflow is a second file that uses the changesets action. It opens a version pull request and publishes when that is merged. It needs an npm token secret, which I added in the repo settings.

I do not want a release yet, since streaming is missing. So the workflow is in place but nothing is published. The CI badge went in the README.

Next: handle doStream for errors that happen before the first chunk.

summary: Wrote a table of which error shapes the classifier accepts, after checking real provider error bodies, and added tests for 529 overloaded and 'overloaded_error'.
body:
I went through error responses from a few providers to see what the classifier misses. Anthropic returns 529 with an overloaded_error type when it is busy, and the SDK does not always mark that as retryable. OpenAI sends 429 for both rate limits and exhausted quota, and the second one will never succeed on retry.

I added a rule for 529 to the classifier, and a check of the error body for overloaded_error. For the quota case I added a check for insufficient_quota, which is treated as not retryable but still a candidate for fallback to another provider. That needs the hook idea from the design note, so I only left a todo and a skipped test.

The tests now use fixtures copied from real bodies, trimmed of ids. 29 tests pass and one is skipped. The table of shapes went into docs/design.md.

summary: Added retries for doStream when the call fails before any chunk is read, and decided that errors after the first chunk are never retried.
body:
Streams are harder, because a call can fail at two points: when doStream itself rejects, and later while the stream is read. Only the first is safe to retry, since after a chunk has reached the user the text cannot be taken back.

I implemented the first case by awaiting doStream inside the same loop used for doGenerate. If it throws a retryable error, backoff and try again, with the same fallback chain. That reused almost all of the code. The loop was already generic over the call, so I made it take a function rather than a method name.

The second case is more subtle. Some providers return a 200 and then put an error part as the first item of the stream. From the outside the call looked successful. I wrapped the returned stream with a reader that peeks at the first part. If that part is an error of a retryable type, the loop treats it as a failure of the call and tries again. If the first part is anything else, it is put back in front and the stream is returned as normal.

Peeking has a cost. The user does not get the stream object until the first part has arrived, which delays the return of doStream slightly. For a language model, the first chunk usually comes quickly, but it can take several seconds on a long prompt. I think this is acceptable and I added a note in the README. A later option could allow turning it off.

Tests use a mock stream built with ReadableStream. Cases: reject then success, error part first then success, error after a text part passes through to the user unchanged, and fallback to another model for a stream. The last case caught a bug where the cancelled first stream was never closed, leaving a dangling reader. I added a cancel call to the peeking code when discarding a stream.

36 tests pass. Next I should check abort signals, because a user cancelling in the middle of a backoff sleep currently has no effect.

summary: Wrote the second half of the README: streaming behavior, which errors are retried, and an honest limitations section.
body:
Spent the session on docs. The streaming section explains that a stream is retried only until the first part arrives, and why. A short example shows streamText with a fallback.

A section lists the errors that count as retryable: 408, 409, 429, 5xx, 529, and network resets. It also says that insufficient_quota is not retried. The limitations section is plain: no retry after the first chunk, no abort handling yet, and no logging.

I reread the whole README as a newcomer would and cut a paragraph that explained jitter at too much length. A link to the AI SDK docs for model setup replaced it. I also ran the code samples through tsc by copying them into a temp file, and fixed one import that was misspelled.

The docs now match the code as of today. Next: abort handling.

summary: Abort signals now stop the retry loop, including during a backoff sleep, and the abort reason is thrown rather than the last model error.
body:
The AI SDK passes an abortSignal in the call options. Before today, the library ignored it between attempts, so a user who aborted during a 20 second backoff still waited for the sleep and then made one more call.

I changed the sleep function to take the signal and reject as soon as it fires. It uses a promise with a timer and an abort listener, and removes the listener when the timer ends so that nothing leaks. The loop also checks signal.aborted before each attempt.

A design question was what to throw. Two choices: the last model error, or the abort reason. I chose the abort reason, because the user asked to stop, and the model error is not why the call ended. If the signal has no reason, the default AbortError from the platform is used. This matches how fetch behaves.

One trap: an abort during an attempt makes the model throw its own error, often an AbortError, which is not retryable. That already stops the loop. But some providers wrap it in an APICallError with isRetryable true. So the loop now checks the signal first and does not retry when it is aborted, whatever the error says.

Tests: abort before the first call gives zero calls, abort in the middle of a sleep returns within a few milliseconds, abort during a call stops without a retry, and the fallback chain stops too. I used real timers with short delays for the sleep test, since the point is the listener. 42 tests pass.

summary: Fixed a listener leak in the abortable sleep found by running the tests with a max-listeners warning turned into an error.
body:
While reading the abort code again I wondered whether the listeners were removed on the success path. A test that makes 30 calls with the same signal printed a MaxListenersExceededWarning, which means they were not.

The cause: the cleanup ran when the signal fired, but not when the timer ended first. The listener stayed on the signal until it was garbage collected with the signal. For one long-lived signal shared across many calls, that adds up.

The fix was a single finish function that clears the timer and removes the listener, called from both paths. I added a test that makes 30 sleeps with one signal and asserts that the listener count is zero afterward, using getEventListeners from node:events. I also made the Node warning an error in the Vitest setup file so that the problem would show up again if it came back.

43 tests pass. A patch changeset was added even though nothing has been published yet.

summary: Added support for the Retry-After header: a delay from the server now replaces the computed backoff when it is longer, within a cap.
body:
Providers often tell the client how long to wait. The AI SDK keeps the response headers on APICallError, so the library can read retry-after-ms first and retry-after second.

The parser handles both forms of Retry-After: a number of seconds and an HTTP date. For a date it computes the difference from now and clamps at zero. A value that is not a number or date is ignored. The millisecond header wins if both are present.

The rule for using it: take the larger of the server's delay and the computed backoff. I considered taking the server value always, but jitter helps when many clients get the same header, so a small random extra is still useful. I settled on using the larger value and adding no jitter on top when the server's value wins.

There is also a cap. A server asking for 10 minutes should not freeze an interactive call. The new option maxRetryAfter defaults to 60000 ms. When the header is above the cap, the library does not wait at all and moves to the next model in the chain, or throws if there is none. That felt better than waiting for a shorter time than asked, which would be sure to hit the limit again.

Tests use a fake clock for the date form. Cases: seconds, milliseconds, date in the past, garbage value, value above the cap with a fallback, and the abort during such a wait. 51 tests pass.

One thing to check later is whether the headers are lowercased by every provider package. I handle both cases for now.

summary: Triaged the AI SDK major version bump: listed the breaking changes that touch the model interface and started a branch-free port on main behind a compatibility type.
body:
A new major version of the AI SDK came out. I read the migration guide and the changelog and listed what affects ai-retry.

The language model interface moved to a new specification version. The call options and the result shape changed in a few places: the stream part types were renamed, usage fields were reorganized, and the specificationVersion string differs. Our code touches the interface in three places: the wrapper model, the stream peeking, and the test mock.

APICallError is still exported and keeps isRetryable and responseHeaders, so the classifier needs no change. That was the part I worried about most.

The plan is to support both majors for a while. Peer dependency becomes a range. The model type is imported from the provider package, and a small adapter file isolates the differences, so the loop and the backoff stay unchanged. I installed the new version as a dev dependency under an alias, so that both can be typechecked in CI.

Today I only added the alias and ran the typecheck against the new version. It shows 9 errors, all in the wrapper and the mock. No code changes yet. Tomorrow's work is the adapter.

summary: Wrote the adapter for the two AI SDK majors; the library now typechecks and passes all tests against both, with CI running a matrix over them.
body:
Created src/compat.ts. It exports the model type and a few helpers: one to read the stream parts in either naming, and one to build a wrapped model that keeps the right specificationVersion of the model it wraps.

The key choice is that the wrapper copies the version string from the inner model rather than hard-coding it. That way a model from either major passes through without being rejected by the SDK's own check. The provider and modelId properties are also forwarded, since users see them in telemetry.

Stream peeking was the main difference. In the older version the first error part had type error with an error field. In the new one the name is the same but the shape of the part around it changed. The helper normalizes both to an object with an error value, and the peeking code uses only that.

The mock model in the tests had to produce either shape. I made the helper take the version as an argument and run the whole suite twice, once per major, with a Vitest project setup. The test count doubles in the report, 51 per version.

While doing this I found that the usage object is not touched by the library at all. Nothing to adapt there, which is a good sign for the design.

CI now installs each major in a matrix leg, next to the Node versions. That makes four legs. A first run failed on one leg because of a lockfile mismatch with the alias; the fix was to install the second major in a separate step with no-save.

All four legs are green. The peer dependency is now a range of both majors. I updated the README with a compatibility note and added a changeset. Next: look at an issue-ready first release.

summary: Prepared and published the first minor release to npm, after a dry run found the type declarations for the CJS build were missing from the exports map.
body:
Today was release preparation. I ran npm pack --dry-run and then installed the tarball in two scratch projects: one ESM and one CJS with TypeScript set to node16 module resolution.

The ESM project worked. The CJS project failed to find types: TS7016 for the package. The exports map listed a types entry only at the top, and node16 resolution wants types inside each condition, with a .d.cts file for the require case. tsdown had created both declaration files, but the map pointed to just one.

I changed the exports so that import and require each have their own types and default entries. I also checked the result with the publint and arethetypeswrong tools. The second one had flagged a problem with masquerading as ESM, and after the change it showed all green for node16, bundler and node10 modes.

The changeset text was cleaned up. It is one entry that lists the features: retry with backoff and jitter, model fallback, stream retry before the first chunk, abort handling, Retry-After, and support for both majors.

I merged the version pull request created by the release workflow, and the publish job ran. It took about two minutes. I checked the page on npm and installed the package from the registry in a clean folder to run the README example with a mock. It worked.

I created a GitHub release with the changelog text. The repo got topics and a short description.

Something I want to do soon: add a small examples folder, since several things in the README are only fragments. There are no issues from users yet, and I have not told anyone beyond a post in my own channels. A fix for a second look at the peek delay is in my notes too.

summary: Added an examples folder with four runnable scripts and a smoke test in CI that runs them against mock providers, catching a stale import in the fallback example.
body:
The README has fragments, and fragments rot. I created examples/ with four scripts: basic retry, fallback across providers, streaming with fallback, and abort with a timeout. Each is a standalone TypeScript file that can run with tsx.

They need a model to call. Real keys in CI are out of the question, so each example reads an environment variable called AI_RETRY_MOCK. When it is set, the script builds a model from the test helper that fails a couple of times and then succeeds. Without it, the script uses the real provider packages. This keeps the code that users read close to what they would write, with the mock hidden in one small function at the top.

I did not like that mock logic in examples, so I put it in examples/_mock.ts and import it only under the variable. The real code path is a plain import of the provider package.

Then a CI step: run all four with the variable set and check that each exits with code 0 and prints the expected last line. Running it locally, the fallback example failed at once. It imported a type called FallbackOption that was renamed to FallbackEntry before the first release. The README had the right name already, and the example had the stale one. The typecheck did not catch it because examples were outside the tsconfig include. I added them to a separate tsconfig that CI checks.

The streaming example prints chunks with a delay, so the smoke test took 9 seconds. I cut the delay in mock mode to 0.

Another small find: the abort example has a 500 ms timeout through AbortSignal.timeout, and with a mock that waits 2 seconds on the first attempt, the call is aborted and the thrown error is a TimeoutError rather than an AbortError. That is correct per the platform, but I added a line in the README on abort reasons, since users checking error.name might be surprised.

The workflow time rose by about 20 seconds per leg. I limited the smoke step to one Node version and one SDK major, which is enough for scripts that only exercise the public API.

A patch changeset was added for the README and the examples. Not yet decided: whether examples should be part of the npm package. I think not, and a files field already excludes them.

summary: First user issue: a report that the stream peek delays doStream by seconds; added a peek option so users can turn it off and documented the tradeoff.
body:
The first real issue arrived. A user streams long answers from a slow reasoning model and says that the call returns only after the first chunk, so their UI shows no sign of progress for several seconds. They saw it was caused by the peeking code.

I reproduced it with a mock that waits 4 seconds before its first part. With the library, doStream resolved after 4 seconds. Without it, doStream resolved at once and the first part arrived after 4 seconds. So the report is right, and it was the same cost I noted in the first design.

There are two ways to deal with it. One is to remove peeking. That loses the retry for providers that send an error part in a 200 stream, which is the less common case but real. The other is an option. I went with an option named peekFirstChunk, defaulting to true so behavior does not change for existing users. When false, doStream resolves as soon as the inner call does, and only a rejection of the call itself is retried.

Implementation was small, a branch around the peek. I wrote tests for both values, including one that checks the resolve time with a short delay and a generous tolerance, and one that makes sure the error part passes to the user when peeking is off.

I also considered a timeout on the peek, so that after N ms the stream is returned anyway. It is attractive, but it complicates the state: if the error part comes later than the timeout, it can no longer be retried. I noted that as a possible later feature and did not build it.

The README now has a short paragraph on the tradeoff with the option shown. I replied on the issue with the explanation and the version that will contain the change. A minor changeset was added.

The user confirmed in a reply that an early build from a branch-free main commit, installed via a git URL, fixed their case.

summary: Released the peekFirstChunk option as a minor version and closed the first user issue after the reporter confirmed it from the registry.
body:
Merged the version pull request, and the release workflow published the new minor. I installed it from the registry in a scratch project and ran the streaming example with a slow mock. doStream resolved immediately with peekFirstChunk set to false.

The changelog entry was generated from the changeset and reads fine. I edited the GitHub release text to add one sentence about when the option makes sense.

The reporter tried the published version and said it works for their UI. I closed the issue. Downloads on npm are small but nonzero, a few dozen a week.

Next in the queue are the logging hooks someone asked about in a comment, and a review of the options types.

summary: Added onRetry and onFallback callbacks to the options after a user asked for logging, with errors in a callback caught so they cannot break a call.
body:
A comment on the earlier issue asked for a way to see retries happening, since failures are otherwise silent and a call just takes longer. I decided on callbacks rather than a built-in logger, so users can use their own tooling.

Two hooks went in. onRetry is called before each wait, with an object containing the error, the attempt number, the model id, and the delay about to be used. onFallback is called when the chain moves to the next model, with the failed model id, the next model id, and the error.

The design question was what happens if a callback throws. A logging bug should not turn a recoverable failure into a failed call. So the loop wraps each callback in try and catch and ignores the error. I thought about reporting it somewhere but could not find a good place, and a swallowed error in a hook is a known tradeoff. The README says so clearly.

The second question was whether the hooks may be async. Supporting a returned promise means awaiting it, which delays the retry. I chose to allow a promise but not to await it, which is fire and forget. A rejected promise is caught with a catch handler so that no unhandled rejection appears. Someone who wants to delay can do that another way.

I also made the delay value in onRetry the real one after Retry-After was applied, not the base backoff. This took a small reorder in the loop: compute the delay, then call the hook, then sleep.

Tests: the hook gets the right arguments across 3 attempts, the fallback hook fires once per switch, a throwing callback does not stop the call, a rejecting async callback causes no unhandled rejection (checked with a process listener), and the hooks do not fire after an abort.

The types for the hook argument are exported as RetryInfo and FallbackInfo. An example for logging with console.warn went into the examples folder, and the smoke test runs it. A minor changeset was added.

summary: Reproduced a user's report that onRetry fired once more than expected on the last attempt; it was by design, but the docs were unclear, so the callback contract is now written down.
body:
A user opened an issue saying that with maxAttempts set to 3, onRetry was called three times, and they expected two, since the third attempt has no retry after it. I reproduced it with a mocked model that always fails with a 429. The callback was called after each failed attempt, including the last one, just before the error was rethrown. That was a mistake in my reading of the name, not a bug in the logic, but the behavior was confusing.

I looked at the code in the retry loop and decided to change it, because a callback named onRetry should only fire when another attempt will actually follow. The call now happens only if attempts remain and the error is retryable. For the final failure the thrown error is the signal, so no callback runs. The attempt number passed to the callback is the one that just failed, starting at 1, and I added that to the type comments.

I updated two existing tests that had encoded the old count and added one for the maxAttempts of 1 case, where the callback must never run. All 31 tests pass. The README section on callbacks now has a short table of when each one fires. Because this changes observable behavior, I added a changeset marked as a patch with a note about it, and replied on the issue with the reasoning and asked the reporter to confirm after the release.

summary: Answered a user question about why a fallback model is never reached after a 400, and wrote the answer into the README as a short FAQ entry.
body:
A user asked on an issue why their fallback was not used when the primary returned a 400 with a context length message. They expected the second model, which has a larger window, to take over.

This is the design from the start: only retryable errors lead to a fallback. A 400 is not retryable, so the chain stops. For their case, the policy is wrong, since a context length error is specific to the model, and another model could succeed.

I explained the default, and then looked at what options exist now. There is a shouldFallback idea in the design note, but it is not built. Today they could write a wrapper around the call themselves, which is not good enough for a library meant to do this.

So I opened a follow-up task: a retryable option that takes a function and gets the error and the model id, and returns true, false, or a string telling whether to retry, fall back, or stop. I did not start it, since the shape needs thought. I asked the user in the issue whether a function with the error as argument would fit their use. They said yes.

In the meantime I added a FAQ section to the README with the question about 400s and the answer that only retryable errors fall back by default, with a note that a configurable policy is planned. The issue stays open and is labeled as an enhancement.

summary: Built the retryable option as a function returning retry, fallback or stop, with the old behavior as default, and tested a context length case end to end.
body:
Started the policy function from the open issue. The option is called shouldRetry, hmm, I settled on classify, which takes an object with the error, the attempt, and the model id, and may return 'retry', 'fallback', or 'stop'. It can also return undefined to use the built-in rule.

The built-in rule is unchanged, so existing users see no difference. A return of 'retry' goes through backoff on the same model, subject to maxAttempts. A return of 'fallback' skips the remaining attempts for this model and moves to the next one at once, with no delay. A return of 'stop' throws the error.

The skip of attempts is the useful part for the reporter. A context length error returns 'fallback' and the larger model is called without waiting.

One point to check was the interaction with abort. The signal check comes before the policy, so an aborted call never reaches classify. Another was a throwing classify function. Here I chose the opposite of the hooks: the error from classify is not swallowed, because a broken policy should be loud. It is thrown with the original error attached as cause.

Tests: each of the three return values, undefined falling back to the default, a throw from classify with its cause, and the context length example through two mock models. 62 tests pass per major.

The README has a new section with the example from the issue. I have to wait for a second look at the type of the returned string before releasing.

summary: Tightened the classify types to a string union with an object form for a custom delay, and updated the tests and README example to match.
body:
On rereading, the return type of classify was just string, so a typo like 'fallbak' compiled and then fell to the default silently. I changed it to a union of the three literals, plus undefined.

While at it I added an object form: { action: 'retry', delay: 5000 } lets the policy set the wait for that attempt. That covers users who want to read a provider-specific field from an error body, which the built-in Retry-After parsing does not know. The custom delay still respects the maxDelay cap, and the abort signal.

I checked how a bare string and the object form are told apart at runtime. It is a typeof check, and an object without a valid action is a thrown error with a clear message, since silently ignoring it would hide bugs.

Type tests now include a negative case for the typo. The runtime tests cover the object form with and without a delay, and the invalid object.

The README example was rewritten to use the typed union. 66 tests pass per major. A changeset marks this as a minor feature together with the earlier work.

summary: Released the classify option and answered the issue; a post-release install check showed the d.cts file missed the new types until a stale build folder was cleaned.
body:
Merged the version pull request for the new minor, which contains the classify option, the readonly types and the fallback detection fix. The publish job succeeded.

As usual I installed the published version in a scratch project. The ESM import compiled. The CJS project with node16 resolution reported that the action union had no member 'fallback', so the types in the d.cts file seemed old. That would have been a bad release.

I unpacked the tarball and looked at dist. The d.cts file did contain the old union. The ESM d.ts file had the new one. So the two declaration builds disagreed.

The cause was in my local flow, not in CI. I had run the release build locally earlier with a stale dist folder, but the published tarball was made by CI, which starts clean. I rechecked: the tarball from CI had the right d.cts too, and the scratch project had cached an older version of the package in its node_modules because the install was done with a lockfile pointing at the earlier version. Running a fresh install with the exact new version number fixed the error.

So nothing was wrong with the release. To avoid fooling myself again, I wrote a small script, scripts/check-install.sh, that makes a temp folder, installs the version given as an argument with no lockfile, and typechecks both an ESM and a CJS sample. I added it as a manual step in the release notes for myself.

I also added a clean step before the build in the npm script, to remove dist, since a stale folder was a real risk even if it was not the cause today.

Then I replied on the issue with the version and an example for the context length case. The reporter tried it and confirmed that the larger model is now used. I closed the issue and updated the FAQ entry, replacing the note about a planned policy with a link to the classify section.

Open items for the next weeks: a look at the docs structure, since the README is getting long, and a review of the error thrown when the whole chain fails.

summary: Added a maxDelay cap to the backoff so a high attempt count can no longer produce multi-minute sleeps, with tests on the clamp and on jitter staying under the cap.
body:
A user comment on the classify issue mentioned that with maxAttempts set to 10 the exponential delay reached several minutes. I added a maxDelay option to the backoff settings, default 30 seconds, applied after the factor is computed and before jitter.

The order mattered. Clamping after jitter made the delays bunch up at the cap, while clamping before keeps the spread. Full jitter now draws from zero to min(maxDelay, base * factor^n).

Validation rejects a maxDelay below the base delay with a clear error when the model is wrapped. That follows the same pattern as the other options.

Tests use the injectable random source: one checks the clamp at attempt 12, another that a random value of 0.999 stays below the cap. The Retry-After path keeps its own separate cap, and I added a test showing the two caps do not interact.

The README options table has a new row. Still to do: decide whether maxDelay should also apply to the classify object form with a custom delay. I lean toward yes but left it for a later entry.

summary: Custom delays from the classify object form are now clamped by maxDelay too, after a test showed a handler returning 10 minutes slept for all of it.
body:
This was the open question from the maxDelay entry. I wrote a failing test first: a classify function returned { action: 'retry', delay: 600000 } and the fake timer advanced the full ten minutes. That is surprising for anyone who set maxDelay as a safety net.

The fix clamps custom delays to maxDelay in the same place the computed backoff is clamped. The Retry-After header already had its own cap, so it is untouched.

I considered letting an explicit custom delay bypass the cap, since the user chose it deliberately. I decided against it because the cap is documented as the upper bound on any single sleep. A user who wants longer sleeps can raise maxDelay.

While in there I noticed the delay resolution was spread over three functions. I merged them into one resolveDelay(error, attempt, classified) that returns a number. The order is now: custom delay, then Retry-After if longer than computed, then backoff, then the clamp.

Tests went from 71 to 78. They cover each source of delay against the cap and the case where maxDelay is lower than the Retry-After cap.

I updated the classify section of the README with a sentence on the clamp. No release yet. I want to batch this with whatever comes next from the issue tracker.

summary: Investigated an issue where fallback models inherited the primary's abort signal listener and found the listener was added once per attempt, so I moved it to once per call.
body:
A user reported a MaxListenersExceededWarning when running a long chain of fallbacks with many attempts. I reproduced it with a script: 5 models, 4 attempts each, and a single AbortSignal shared with the caller.

The cause was in the attempt loop. Each attempt called signal.addEventListener to wire up the abortable sleep, and the removal only ran on the success path. Failed attempts that went straight to the next sleep left their listeners attached until the call ended. The fix from the earlier leak was correct for the sleep itself, but not for this outer wiring.

I moved the listener setup to the top of the call, with a single abort promise that every sleep and attempt races against. A finally block removes it once. The count in the repro dropped from 20 listeners to 1.

I added a test that wraps the signal in a counting proxy and asserts at most one listener is attached at any time, across both success and failure paths. It would have caught this.

I also checked doStream, which has the same structure. It showed the same issue and received the same fix. Both paths now share a helper, withAbort, in abort.ts.

The reporter was thanked on the issue and told a patch would follow. I did not release yet; a patch is next.

summary: Released the listener fix as a patch version and confirmed from a clean install that the warning is gone in the user's repro script.
body:
I ran the full test suite and the CI matrix across both AI SDK majors, then created the changeset as a patch with a note about the listener fix and the maxDelay clamp. The maxDelay change is technically new behavior, so I called it out as a minor instead. The version bump became a minor.

Before publishing, I cleaned the build folder first. The earlier release had a stale d.cts problem, so I now remove dist before every build in the release script. I added that as a prebuild step so nobody has to remember it.

After publishing I installed the package into a fresh temp directory and ran the reporter's script with --trace-warnings. No warning appeared with 5 models and 4 attempts. I also ran it with 20 models to be sure.

The type declarations loaded for both ESM and CJS consumers. I checked with a tiny tsc run for each module setting.

I replied on the issue with the version number and asked the reporter to confirm. I closed it after they did an hour later.

Nothing else is pending from the tracker. Next I want to look at timeouts as a retryable case.

summary: Wrote down a plan for per-attempt timeouts: an option that aborts a single attempt, treats it as retryable, and leaves the caller's own signal separate.
body:
Two users asked in different issues for a way to cut off a slow call and move on. Today I only planned it.

The design is a timeout option in milliseconds, applied per attempt. Each attempt gets its own AbortController, linked to the caller's signal. If the timer fires, the attempt is aborted and the error is classified as a retryable timeout. If the caller's signal fires, nothing is retried and the abort reason is thrown, as now.

The tricky point is telling the two apart. I will use a dedicated TimeoutError class and check the caller's signal first.

For streams the timeout covers only the time until the first chunk, because later errors are never retried anyway. Open question: whether the fallback should get a fresh timeout. I think yes, it is per attempt. Implementation starts tomorrow.

summary: Implemented the per-attempt timeout for doGenerate with a linked abort controller and a TimeoutError that the classifier treats as retryable.
body:
I added the timeout option and a TimeoutError class exported from the package. Each attempt now creates its own AbortController. The caller's signal is linked to it so a user abort still cancels the attempt immediately.

The order of checks after a failed attempt is: if the caller's signal is aborted, throw its reason. Otherwise, if the attempt's timer fired, wrap the error as a TimeoutError and classify it. Getting this order wrong would have made user aborts look like timeouts and be retried. A test covers exactly that case.

The timer is cleared in a finally block. The tests use fake timers, and I confirmed with vi.getTimerCount() that none are left pending after success, failure or abort.

Option validation requires a positive finite number. Zero throws, since it would mean an instant timeout, which is almost certainly a mistake.

The classifier gets one new rule: TimeoutError is retryable with the normal backoff. Users can still override this through the classify option.

Tests rose from 78 to 87. doStream is next. It needs the timeout to cover only the wait for the first chunk.

summary: Added the first-chunk timeout to doStream and found that cancelling the underlying stream reader was needed, or the provider connection stayed open after a timeout.
body:
For doStream the timeout covers the peek of the first chunk. If it fires before a chunk arrives, the attempt is aborted and counted as a retryable TimeoutError. Once the first chunk is read, the timer is cleared and never applies again.

My first version aborted the controller but did not cancel the reader. In the mock this looked fine. When I wrote a stricter mock that tracks whether cancel was called on the stream, the test failed: the stream was left open. With a real provider that would leave a socket hanging until the server gave up.

The fix calls reader.cancel() with the timeout error in the failure path, wrapped in a catch since cancel can reject on an already errored stream. The same cancel applies when the first chunk contains an error part and we decide to retry.

I added three tests: timeout before first chunk then success on the second attempt, timeout on all attempts rethrowing the last TimeoutError, and a slow stream after the first chunk that is not cut off.

The peekFirstChunk option set to false skips peeking, so there is no first chunk to wait for. In that case the timeout has nothing to cover. I made the validation warn in the docs rather than throw: timeout has no effect on streams when peekFirstChunk is false.

The retry loop for streams is now fairly long. I left a TODO to extract it, but not today.

summary: Wrote the README section on timeouts, including the interaction with abort signals and the peekFirstChunk limitation for streams, and added an example script.
body:
I added a Timeouts section to the README after the Abort section. It explains that the timeout is per attempt, not for the whole call, and shows a three-line example with a 10 second timeout and a fallback model.

A short table lists what happens in each case: the timeout fires, the caller aborts, and the attempt fails with another error. The caller's abort always wins, and I made that explicit.

For streams the doc says the timeout only covers waiting for the first chunk, and that setting peekFirstChunk to false disables it. That is the honest answer, and I put it in the limitations section as well.

I also added a fifth script to the examples folder, timeout-fallback.ts, which uses a mock provider that sleeps. The CI smoke test runs it, and it passed on the first try, finishing in under a second with a 50 ms timeout.

The options table now has a timeout row with the type and default of undefined. The onRetry callback doc mentions that the error passed in can now be a TimeoutError.

No release today. I want to check one more thing in the classify option before shipping.

summary: Checked that the classify function receives TimeoutError and can turn it into a fallback, and added the test and a README line showing how.
body:
Users of the classify option should be able to say that a timeout means moving on to the fallback rather than trying the same model again. I wrote a test where classify returns 'fallback' for TimeoutError and confirmed it.

The test passed straight away because TimeoutError goes through the same classification path as other errors. Still, it was worth pinning down as a test, since the timeout code wraps errors in a special case.

One gap showed up: the context object passed to classify has the attempt number and model id, but not whether the error came from the timeout or the provider. Users can use instanceof TimeoutError, which is exported, so I left the context alone.

The README classify example now shows the timeout case in three lines. I also reran the full matrix over both AI SDK majors locally; all 90 tests pass.

The changeset is written as a minor. Release is planned for tomorrow after a last look at the type output.

summary: Released the timeout option as a minor version, with the pre-build cleanup catching nothing this time and the install check passing for ESM and CJS.
body:
I ran the release script after the CI run on main was green. The prebuild step removed dist, the build ran, and the changesets action produced the version bump to the next minor.

After publishing I did the install check in a temp directory. A TypeScript file imported TimeoutError and used the timeout option, compiled with moduleResolution node16 for both a CJS and an ESM project. Both compiled without errors.

I also ran the examples against the published package rather than the local build. The timeout-fallback script finished correctly.

I commented on the two issues that asked for this and linked the release. One reporter replied within the hour that it worked with their slow provider.

The changelog entry mentions that timeout on streams covers only the first chunk. I also noted the new exported class. Nothing is left open from this topic. Next I plan to look at the issue about the options types.

summary: Reproduced a user's complaint that option types reject a model id string in the fallback list, and traced it to an overly narrow generic that I loosened.
body:
The issue said that passing a string like 'openai/gpt-4o' in the models array produced a type error, although the README example used a model object. I first thought it was a docs mistake. It was not, since the earlier version of the types had accepted strings through the gateway form.

The cause was in the generic constraint I had tightened when the classify types changed. The models option was typed as LanguageModelV2[] only, dropping the union with string. At runtime strings still worked because the AI SDK resolves them, but the types said otherwise.

I added a type-level test file using expectTypeOf from Vitest. It asserts that both a model object and a string are accepted, and that a number is rejected. The test failed before the fix and passed after.

The fix widened the type to a union and added a small resolver in the wrapper that turns strings into models using the SDK's resolver for whichever major is installed. The adapter handles this for both majors, but the older major needed a different import.

I checked the d.ts output by hand. The union appears as expected and no any leaks in.

Another type problem turned up on the way: onFallback's callback parameter typed the model as unknown. I typed it as the resolved model. This is a small breaking change for anyone who cast it, but the cast would still compile.

I ran the whole matrix and then wrote a reply on the issue asking the reporter to confirm with a pre-release build. A patch release goes out once they do.

summary: The reporter confirmed the string model fix with a pre-release build, so I shipped it as a patch and closed the issue.
body:
I published a pre-release tag to npm with the type widening and asked the reporter to try it. They answered after a couple of hours that the string form compiled in their project and that onFallback now showed the model type.

Then I wrote the changeset as a patch and released it. The prebuild cleanup ran again and the install check against a fresh directory passed for ESM and CJS.

One detail from the reporter's project: they used a strict tsconfig with exactOptionalPropertyTypes. I tested that flag as well and found that passing timeout: undefined explicitly failed the type check. I changed the option types to accept undefined for every optional field. That went into the same patch before publishing, with a new type test.

I added exactOptionalPropertyTypes and noUncheckedIndexedAccess to the type test tsconfig so these cases are covered from now on.

The issue is closed. The pre-release tag was removed from npm dist-tags to avoid confusion.

summary: Designed and built a logging hook upgrade: onRetry and onFallback now receive a single event object with attempt, delay, model and error, while the old positional form keeps working.
body:
A user asked for the delay and model id in the onRetry callback, since logging only the error was not enough. The current signature takes the error and the attempt number. Adding more positional arguments would get ugly quickly.

I decided on an event object as the first argument: { error, attempt, delay, modelId, maxAttempts }. To avoid a breaking change, the callbacks are still called with (error, attempt) in the old order, and the event is passed as a third argument. New code can destructure the third parameter.

I wasn't happy with that shape at first. It is a bit odd to have the same data twice. I considered a major version, but the library is young and a breaking change for a logging nicety felt wrong. The README now says the third argument is preferred and the first two are kept for compatibility.

The delay in the event is the value that will actually be slept, after Retry-After, custom delay and the maxDelay clamp. This required computing the delay before calling the callback, which I had been doing after. The reorder is safe since a throwing callback is caught anyway.

For onFallback the event holds the failed model id, the next model id and the error.

Tests check that the old arguments are unchanged, that the event delay equals the delay the fake timer waits, and that a throwing callback still doesn't break the call.

I also added the types for the event to the exports. I updated the README's callback contract section that I wrote some time ago. The table of event fields is short.

Next: examples and a release.

summary: Released the event object for the logging hooks as a minor version and updated the logging example to print delay and model id.
body:
I changed the logging example script to destructure the third argument and print a line like 'retry 2/4 on gpt-4o after 840ms'. The smoke test in CI runs it against mock providers and checks that the output contains the delay.

Before releasing I reran the matrix across both AI SDK majors and the type tests. All 101 tests passed.

I wrote the changeset as a minor and noted that positional arguments remain supported. After the release I ran the usual install check in a clean directory with both module formats, and the d.cts file contained the event type.

The user who asked for it got a reply with the version and a snippet. They answered with a thumbs up and a question about structured logging with pino. I explained that the event is a plain object and can be passed straight to a logger. I did not add a pino integration since that belongs in user code.

I also searched the open issues and found nothing else pending. The next topic from my own list is a docs pass, since several questions in issues were answered by the README already.

summary: Did a docs pass over the README after counting that four recent questions were already answered in it, and reorganized it so the FAQ and the error table are easier to find.
body:
Four issues in the last weeks asked things that the README answered, just not where people looked. I took that as a sign of a structure problem rather than a reader problem.

The README had grown to about 400 lines. I moved the options table up right after the basic example and added a small table of contents at the top. The long sections on streaming and abort stayed, but I shortened each by cutting repeated explanations.

The FAQ now has six questions: why a fallback is not reached after a 400, why a stream error after the first chunk is not retried, why onRetry fires on the last attempt, how timeouts interact with abort, how to use string model ids, and how to log with the event object. Each answer is two or three sentences with a link to the relevant section.

I checked every code block by pasting it into a scratch file and compiling it. Two examples were stale: one still used the old classify return values from before the string union, and one imported a type that had been renamed. I fixed both.

To stop this recurring, I wrote a small script, docs-check.ts, that extracts the typescript code blocks from the README and typechecks them against the built types. It runs in CI after the build. It failed on its first run because of a snippet with ellipses, so I allowed a marker comment to skip a block.

The CI run is green. Docs changes need no release, since the README on npm updates with the next one. I may want a patch just to refresh it.

summary: Looked into a user report that fallback ran after an error with a 422 status that should not retry, and found the classifier matched the word 'overloaded' anywhere in the message.
body:
The report: a request with an invalid schema returned 422 with a body that mentioned 'overloaded' in a validation message about a function name. The library treated it as an overload error and moved to the fallback model, which then failed the same way.

The classifier looked at the status code first and then fell back to matching strings in the error message. A 422 has no retryable status, so it reached the string match and found 'overloaded'. That was too loose.

I changed the order of rules. If a status code is present and is a known non-retryable 4xx, other than 408, 409 and 429, the classifier returns stop without looking at the message. The string match remains only for errors with no status, for example network layer errors and some streaming error parts.

I added tests with the reporter's exact body, plus 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 with 'overloaded' and 'rate limit' in the message. All should stop. A 429 and 529 with the same text still retry.

I also reread the classifier table I wrote earlier from real provider bodies. It stated that the message match is a fallback, but I had not made the status precedence explicit there. I updated the table.

The fix goes out as a patch. I told the reporter and asked for their body in case other shapes exist.

summary: Released the classifier precedence fix as a patch and added a regression test file that holds real error bodies from user reports.
body:
After CI passed, I released the fix as a patch with a changeset that describes the behavior change plainly: non-retryable 4xx statuses no longer fall through to message matching.

I created a fixtures folder for the classifier tests, with one JSON file per real error body that a user or I have seen: the 422 from this report, the 529 overloaded body, a 400 context length error and a gateway timeout page in HTML. The test iterates over the files and compares the classification with an expected value stored in the same file.

The point of the folder is that a future bug report becomes a file and a line, not a new hand-written mock. I documented that in CONTRIBUTING.md in three sentences.

The reporter answered with a second body, a 400 that mentioned 'rate limit' in a field name. It was correctly stopped by the new rule, and I added it as a fixture.

Post release install check passed for both module formats. The issue was closed after the reporter confirmed.

summary: Planned the breaking change for the next major: removing positional callback arguments and the old classify return values, with a migration guide drafted before any code.
body:
The event object for the hooks left some baggage: the positional arguments in onRetry and onFallback are kept only for compatibility. Together with the deprecated classify values, it is time to plan a clean major release.

I listed what would change. First, the callbacks receive only the event object. Second, the boolean return of retryable, which is still accepted, goes away; only the string union and object forms remain. Third, the default for peekFirstChunk stays as is. Fourth, the minimum Node version moves to 20, since 18 is out of support and CI no longer tests it.

I considered also dropping the older AI SDK major. I decided against it for this release: the adapter costs little and several users are still on that major. It can go in a later one with its own announcement.

Before writing code, I drafted MIGRATION.md with a before and after snippet for each change. Writing the guide first showed that the boolean return removal affects the most users, so I will keep a clear thrown error: if retryable returns a boolean, the error message says what to return instead. That is friendlier than silent misbehavior.

I checked npm download stats for versions to estimate who is on old versions. Most downloads are on the latest two minors, which is reassuring.

The plan has five steps: deprecation warnings in a final minor, the code changes, the migration guide, a release candidate, and the final release. The deprecation warning step comes first. It logs once per process through console.warn when a boolean is returned or when callbacks use positional arguments. The warning can be silenced with an environment variable.

I added the plan as a checklist in an issue pinned in the repository so users can comment.

Tomorrow I start with the deprecation minor.

summary: Added the one-time deprecation warnings for boolean returns and positional callback arguments, with an environment variable to silence them.
body:
The warnings come from a small helper, warnOnce(key, message), which keeps a Set of keys in module scope and calls console.warn only the first time. There are two keys: one for boolean returns from the retryable option and one for callbacks that read the positional arguments.

Detecting positional use of callbacks is not possible in general, since a function can ignore its arguments. I settled on checking function length: a callback declared with two or more parameters triggers the warning. That is a heuristic and will miss some cases, but it also warns for anyone who declared the third parameter and the first two. I made the message specific so those users know what to change.

The environment variable AI_RETRY_NO_DEPRECATION silences everything. Tests for the helper reset the Set between cases through an exported internal function that I did not add to the public types.

I ran the full suite with warnings captured through a spy. Existing tests that use booleans now trigger the warning, which is fine, but noisy, so I silenced it in the test setup file and added dedicated tests for the warning itself.

The changeset is a minor. The migration guide is linked from the warning text. I will release tomorrow after checking the warning output in the examples.

summary: Released the deprecation minor and found that the warning fired for the library's own examples, so I updated them to the new forms before publishing.
body:
Running the examples folder with warnings visible showed that two of the five scripts still used a boolean retryable and positional callbacks. They would have warned on every user's first run of the examples, which is a poor look right after a deprecation notice.

I changed both scripts to the string union and the event object. The smoke test in CI now sets the variable that turns warnings into errors, a flag I added in the test setup only, so any example that triggers a deprecation fails the build.

The README had two snippets with the old forms that docs-check does not catch, as they are valid code. I fixed those by hand and added a grep step in CI for the old patterns in README and examples.

Then I released the minor. The install check passed. I ran the examples from the published package and saw no warnings.

I posted on the pinned issue that the deprecation release is out, with the date left open for the major. One user commented asking whether the boolean form would be supported through an adapter; I said no, because the migration is one line, and showed the line.

Next is the code change for the major, starting with removals.

summary: Removed the deprecated boolean return and positional callback arguments from the source, replacing the boolean case with a thrown error that tells the user what to return.
body:
I started the major with the removals. In the classification code, a boolean returned from retryable now throws an AiRetryConfigError with a message like: 'retryable returned true; return "retry", "fallback" or "stop" instead'. This is thrown on the first call rather than being treated silently as a stop.

The callbacks now get only the event object. The code that called them with (error, attempt, event) is simplified to a single argument. This removed about 40 lines, including the warnOnce paths, which I deleted along with the environment variable.

Many tests used the old forms. I updated 23 of them by hand and deleted 4 that existed only to cover the compatibility behavior. The test count fell from 112 to 108, with 3 new ones for the config error.

The type definitions lost the union with boolean and the positional signature. The type tests confirm that a boolean return is now a compile error, which is the best outcome for TypeScript users: they find out before running.

I bumped the engines field to Node 20 and removed Node 18 from the docs. CI already ran only 20 and 22.

The diff is large but mostly deletion. I made sure the migration guide matches the final behavior and corrected the error message text in it. The changeset is marked major.

One item is left: a release candidate for users to try.

summary: Published a release candidate of the major under the next tag and asked the people from the pinned issue to try it, with a checklist of what to look for.
body:
I published the major as a release candidate under the npm tag 'next', so a plain install still gets the stable minor. The prebuild cleanup ran and the post-publish check in a temp directory passed for ESM and CJS, which I did again on the next tag specifically.

On the pinned issue I posted install instructions, a link to MIGRATION.md, and a short checklist: does it compile, does the config error appear if a boolean is still returned, do your logs still show delay and model id, and does anything behave differently with timeouts or abort.

I tried the migration myself on a scratch project that used the old forms. It took about five minutes and the compile errors pointed exactly where the changes were needed. The one confusing point was the callback: the error said the parameter had too many properties missing. I added a line to the guide that shows how to destructure the event.

While testing I noticed the example in the guide for the object form of classify used a delay in seconds by mistake; the option is in milliseconds. I corrected it, and I checked the README for the same slip. It was fine there.

Two users have already replied. One migrated in a few minutes without trouble. The other uses the older AI SDK major and reported that the string model ids resolve correctly there too, which I had only tested in the matrix.

I will wait several days for feedback before the final release. Meanwhile I'm leaving the code alone.

summary: Feedback on the release candidate found one real bug, a type error with a readonly models array, which I fixed and published as a second candidate.
body:
A user who migrated reported that passing a readonly tuple, declared with as const, to the models option failed to compile. The type was a mutable array, so readonly arrays were rejected, although the library never mutates the list.

I reproduced it in a type test with expectTypeOf and an as const array. It failed with the same message the user quoted. This was an old problem, not new in the major, but it only surfaced now because the user's migration touched that code.

The fix changed the option to readonly arrays of models, which accepts both readonly and mutable arrays. Inside the library the code copies the list once at wrapping time, so later changes to the caller's array do not affect a running call. I added a test for that behavior as well, since it was an implicit property before.

I checked the other array options for the same problem. The list of retryable status codes had it too, so I fixed that as well.

The second release candidate went out under the next tag, and the usual install check passed. I answered the reporter, who confirmed it compiled in under an hour.

No other issues came in on the pinned thread. I plan to give it a few more days and then release the final major.

summary: Third release candidate of the major went out after a docs fix; no new bug reports came in from the pinned issue, so the final release is next.
body:
Published the third candidate under the next tag. It carried only a README correction: the migration guide still showed the old boolean return for the retryable option in one snippet, which a tester had copied and then hit the new thrown error.

I went through the guide line by line and ran every snippet as a script against the built package. Two snippets used positional callback arguments, which no longer work, so I rewrote them to the event object form. All snippets now run clean.

The pinned issue has four people who tried the second candidate. Three said it worked with no changes beyond the migration steps. One asked whether the thrown error for boolean returns could include a link to the guide. I added the link to the message and a test that checks the message mentions the option name.

I also checked the install for ESM and CJS from a clean folder, after removing dist first, because the stale build problem has bitten before. Types resolved in both.

Plan: wait a few days for more feedback, then write the changeset for the major, cut the release notes from the migration guide, and publish under latest. Nothing else is open on the milestone.

summary: Released the major version as latest with release notes taken from the migration guide, and the install check passed for both module formats.
body:
No new reports arrived on the third candidate, so I released the major today. The changeset described the removal of boolean returns and positional callback arguments, and the release notes link to the migration guide.

Before publishing I ran the full Vitest suite and the type tests, then built from a clean dist. The packed tarball was installed in a temp project and imported as ESM and required as CJS. Both worked, and the d.ts and d.cts files contained the event object types.

After publishing I moved the latest tag to the new version and checked npm showed it. I commented on the pinned issue with the version and thanked the testers.

The old major line stays on its own tag with no further work planned except a critical fix. I noted this in the README under a short support section.

summary: A user reported that the major release broke their custom classify handler returning undefined; traced it to a missing default and fixed it with a clear fallback to the built-in classifier.
body:
An issue came in a few hours after the major: a user's classify handler returned undefined for errors it did not care about, and the library now threw the error meant for old boolean returns. Before the major, undefined meant use the default behavior, and I had not kept that in the removal.

I reproduced it with a small test: a handler with an if for 429 and no else. On the new version the call failed with the thrown message about what to return. The user was right that this is a regression and not an intended break, since the migration guide never said undefined was removed.

The cause was in the code that validates the handler result. I had replaced the old boolean branch with a check that threw for any value outside the string union and the object form. Undefined fell into that branch.

The fix treats undefined as no opinion and passes the error to the built-in classifier. Null gets the same treatment. Booleans still throw with the helpful message, since those really were removed.

I added tests for undefined, null, a boolean, and a number. The number case throws with the same message as before. I also updated the types so the handler return type includes undefined and void, because the user wrote the handler without an explicit return and TypeScript complained in a strict config.

The README section on classify now says that returning nothing means use the default. I added a line to the migration guide as well.

Plan: publish as a patch tomorrow morning after the reporter tries a pre-release build. I asked them to install it from the pkg preview of the branch build and report back.

summary: Closed the major release cycle by checking the pinned issue, bumping the npm dist-tags, and writing a short list of follow-ups that came out of the release candidate feedback.
body:
The final release of the major version is two days old, so this session was about closing the loose ends of the whole cycle. I started by reading the pinned issue from top to bottom. Every person who tried a release candidate had replied, and nobody reported anything that was still open. I closed the pinned issue with a short thank-you and a link to the release notes.

Next I checked the npm dist-tags with npm dist-tag ls. The next tag still pointed at the third release candidate, which would confuse anyone who installs with that tag, so I moved it to the same version as latest. I then ran a clean install of ai-retry@latest in a scratch folder and imported it from both an ESM and a CJS script. Both worked, and the d.ts and d.cts files exposed the same exports.

After that I went through the issues that came in during the release candidate period and sorted them into three groups. The first group was already fixed: the readonly models array type error and the docs fix. The second group was questions that the README answers, and for those I added links in my replies. The third group was ideas that I did not want to lose: a total time budget across attempts, a hard deadline per call, and a way to retry when the response is a bad JSON body.

I wrote these three ideas into a short list in the repository notes file, each with the name of the user who asked and the issue number. I also noted that the callback contract in the README should be re-read once more, because the positional form is gone and two examples still mention it in a comment. I fixed those two comments right away, and the fix goes out with the next release. The test suite passed, 212 tests in about 9 seconds. Next I plan to look at the Retry-After question that one user raised in a comment, because it touches the maxDelay cap.

summary: Answered a question on whether the Retry-After header is honored when it is larger than maxDelay; it is capped, and the README now says so.
body:
A user asked why their calls slept less than the Retry-After value of 60 seconds from the provider. The reason is that maxDelay caps every delay, including the one from the header, which I added in the cap work earlier.

I confirmed it with a test that mocks a 429 with the header set to 60 and maxDelay of 10 seconds; the sleep was 10 seconds. That is the intended behavior, but the README only mentioned the cap in the backoff section.

I added a sentence to the Retry-After section and to the options table. I also noted how to raise the cap if the user wants to honor long headers fully.

The user asked whether there should be an option to fail instead of sleeping when the header is above the cap. I opened a small issue to think about it, without committing to build it. It could be done through classify already by returning stop for those errors, so I put that example in the answer.

summary: Added a README recipe showing how to stop instead of waiting when Retry-After exceeds the cap, using classify, with a test that the recipe works.
body:
Following the question about long Retry-After values, I wrote the recipe in the README. The classify handler reads the header from the error response headers, and if it is larger than a threshold, returns stop.

I put the recipe into a test first so the docs cannot drift. The test mocks a 429 with a header of 120 and checks that the call fails after one attempt with the original error and without sleeping.

While doing this I noticed the header name lookup was case sensitive in my test helper but not in the library, which lowercases keys. I made the helper match so the test reflects what real providers send.

The issue about a dedicated option got a comment pointing to the recipe. I will leave it open for a while to see if anyone else wants it. No code change in the library itself was needed.

summary: Investigated a user report of a doubled first attempt with streams and found the peek helper called doStream twice when the first chunk was empty.
body:
A user said their provider was billed twice for some streaming calls. I reproduced it with a mock stream whose first chunk was an empty text delta.

The peek logic read the first chunk, decided it was empty, and then restarted the call as if it had failed before the first chunk. An empty delta is a valid chunk, so the call should have continued.

The cause was a check on chunk content length instead of on whether any chunk had arrived. I changed it to look only at whether the read returned a chunk or the stream ended or errored.

I added tests for an empty first delta, for a stream-start metadata chunk first, and for an immediate end of stream, which still counts as a failure before output. The suite passes.

I asked the user for their provider name to check whether this matched their setup, and I will wait for a reply before releasing.

summary: Released the empty first chunk fix as a patch after the reporter confirmed that their billing duplicates stopped in a test run.
body:
The reporter replied quickly: their provider sends a metadata chunk first, which matched the second test case. They ran a pre-release build against a few hundred calls and saw no doubled requests.

I wrote the changeset as a patch, ran the suite, built from a clean dist, and checked the install for both formats. Published and verified on npm.

I closed the issue and added a line in the README stream section saying that any chunk, including empty ones and metadata, counts as the first chunk. That was a gap in the docs.

Nothing else is pending on streams.

summary: Planned a retry budget option that limits total time across attempts, after a user asked for a hard deadline per call.
body:
A user wants calls to give up after a fixed total time, no matter how many attempts remain. The per-attempt timeout does not cover that, since many attempts plus delays can add up.

I wrote a plan in the issue. The option would be called totalTimeout, in milliseconds. It starts when the call starts, and before each sleep the library checks the time left. If the delay would pass the deadline, it stops and throws the last error instead of sleeping.

Questions I settled in the plan: the deadline does not abort an attempt already running, since that is the job of the per-attempt timeout; the thrown error is the last real error, not a new one, with a flag on it for the deadline; fallbacks share the same budget.

The interaction with the abort signal stays the same: the caller's signal wins at any time.
