I will implement it next, starting with doGenerate and then doStream.

summary: Implemented totalTimeout for generate and stream calls, checking the remaining budget before each sleep, with fake timer tests for the edge cases.
body:
Built the option as planned. A helper holds the start time and returns the time left, and the retry loop asks it before each sleep. If the planned delay is larger than the time left, the loop throws the last error.

I decided to clamp rather than throw when the delay is only slightly too long? No, I kept it simple: if the delay does not fit, stop. Clamping would produce an attempt right at the deadline that is unlikely to finish.

Tests with Vitest fake timers cover these: a budget smaller than the first delay, which gives one attempt only; a budget that fits two attempts; fallback to another model sharing the budget; and an abort signal firing during a sleep.

For streams the same helper is used for failures before the first chunk. After the first chunk nothing is retried anyway.

The error gets a property deadlineExceeded set to true, and the type is exported. The suite passes and the type tests include the new option.

Next: the README section and the release.

summary: Wrote the totalTimeout docs and released it as a minor version, with an install check for both module formats passing.
body:
I wrote the README section for totalTimeout with a short example and a table row. It explains that the budget includes sleeps and attempts, that a running attempt is not cut off, and how it works with the per-attempt timeout. A combined example uses both: five seconds per attempt and twenty seconds in total.

I also added a line on the deadlineExceeded flag and how to check for it in an error handler.

The changeset is a minor. I ran the suite, built from a clean dist, packed the tarball, and installed it in a temp project. ESM import and CJS require both worked, and the d.cts file had the new option type.

Published and verified on npm. I commented on the issue with the version and asked the requester to try it.

One small thing found during the docs: the example script for timeouts used an old option name left over from the first draft. I corrected it and ran the script against a mock.

summary: The requester confirmed totalTimeout works in their app, and I closed the issue and tidied the example scripts folder.
body:
The requester ran the new version in staging and reported that slow provider days no longer produce calls lasting minutes. They set twenty seconds in total and ten per attempt.

I closed the issue. They also noticed that the error message after the deadline did not say that the budget was the cause, only the original error text. I considered changing the message but decided against it, since wrapping the original error would break checks users already have. The flag is the documented way, and I added it to the FAQ.

While here I tidied the examples folder: each script now has a header comment saying what it shows and how to run it, and a shared mock helper replaced three copies.

I ran every example once to check that they still work.

summary: A user hit an unhandled rejection when the caller aborted during a backoff sleep; the sleep timer promise was rejected twice, and the fix settles it once.
body:
A user reported an unhandled promise rejection in Node when they aborted a call during the wait between attempts. The process warning showed an AbortError with no catch.

I reproduced it with a test that aborts while the loop sleeps. The sleep helper listens for the abort event and rejects, and also rejects from a cleanup path after the timer is cleared. The second rejection had no handler.

The fix makes the helper settle once: it removes the listener and clears the timer in one function, and a flag guards against a second settle. I also made sure the listener is removed on normal completion, which was not always the case and could leak on long lived signals.

Tests added: abort during sleep, abort before sleep starts, abort exactly as the timer fires, and a check that the signal has no listeners left after a normal sleep.

I ran Node with the unhandled rejection mode set to throw to make sure the suite would catch this next time, and added it to the test script.

The patch will go out tomorrow after the reporter checks a pre-release.

summary: Released the abort during sleep fix as a patch, then audited all places that add abort listeners and found one more leak in the stream path.
body:
The reporter confirmed that the unhandled rejection is gone, so I released the patch. The changeset, suite, clean build, and install check for ESM and CJS all passed, and I verified the version on npm.

After the release I did the audit I had planned, because this is the second bug about abort listeners after the per-call listener fix earlier. I searched the source for addEventListener and AbortController and made a list of seven places.

Six were fine: each removes its listener in a finally block or uses the once option. The seventh is in the stream path. When a stream fails before the first chunk and the loop moves on to the next attempt, the linked controller from the first-chunk timeout is not aborted or cleaned, so its listener on the caller signal stays until the call ends.

It does not break behavior, but with many attempts it adds listeners, and Node can warn at eleven. With the default of three attempts it is unlikely, and with a high attempt count it would show.

I wrote a test that sets maxAttempts to fifteen with failing streams and counts listeners on the signal using getEventListeners from node events. It failed with fourteen leftover listeners.

The fix puts the cleanup in a finally block around each attempt. The same test now shows zero after the call ends and at most one during an attempt.

I also added a general helper, withLinkedSignal, that creates the controller, links it, and returns a dispose function. All three places that linked signals now use it, so the pattern is in one file.

The suite passes. I will release this as a patch after a day of no other reports. No user has hit it yet, so there is no hurry.

summary: Released the linked signal cleanup as a patch and added a listener count check to the shared test helpers so every abort test asserts a clean signal.
body:
I released the cleanup of the stream path as a patch. The changeset says that it fixes listeners that built up with many attempts, with no behavior change.

The suite and the type tests passed, and the clean build and install check for both formats went well. Verified on npm.

Then I turned the listener count check into a helper, expectNoListeners, in the shared test utilities. The abort tests now call it at the end. Four of the older tests were updated, and none failed, which is good news about the earlier fixes.

I wanted to know whether the helper would catch the bug it was built for, so I temporarily removed the finally block in the stream path. Two tests failed with the listener counts in the message. I restored the block.

An unrelated cleanup: the test for timeouts used real timers with a short sleep, which made it flaky once on CI. I switched it to fake timers.

Nothing else is open for abort handling. I will go back to the user issues next.

summary: Investigated a request to retry on bad JSON responses from the model and found that the schema validation error is thrown outside the library's reach for generateObject.
body:
A user asked for retries when the model returns invalid JSON for generateObject. I looked at how the AI SDK handles it. The parsing and schema validation happen in generateObject after the model call returns, so the library, which wraps the model, never sees that error. The model call itself succeeded.

I confirmed this with a mock model that returns text that is not JSON. The library saw one successful doGenerate and returned it. The error came later from the SDK function.

There are two options. The first is a hook in the library that validates the output in doGenerate with the schema, which means duplicating SDK logic and knowing about the schema, which the model layer does not get in all cases. The second is to document a pattern: the user wraps the generateObject call in their own loop, or uses the SDK's own repair option for text.

I tried the first option in a spike for the case where the response format is json. The call options include the response format and sometimes a schema. A validation function could check that the text parses as JSON and nothing more. That catches broken JSON but not schema violations.

The spike worked for broken JSON: a test with a truncated object triggered a retry and the second response parsed. But it adds a new failure class for something many users do not expect from a model wrapper, and it would double the cost for responses that are valid JSON but wrong against the schema.

I decided to offer it as an opt-in, validateResponse, a function that receives the result and may throw a retryable error. The user decides what to check. That keeps the library out of schema knowledge.

I wrote the design in the issue and asked the requester if this would fit. Next step is to build it if they agree.

summary: Built the opt-in validateResponse option for generate calls, where a thrown error counts as retryable, with tests for fallback and the attempt count.
body:
The requester agreed that a function they control is what they need. I built validateResponse for doGenerate only.

The function receives the result of the model call. If it throws, the error is treated like any failure: it goes through classify, then the retry or fallback logic. A new error class, InvalidResponseError, wraps what the user throws if it is not already an Error, and the default classification is retry.

A decision: the validation also runs for the fallback models. It would be surprising if the fallback result skipped the check. The last attempt that fails validation throws the validation error to the caller.

Tests cover a passing validation, a failing one followed by a pass, all attempts failing, a fallback model whose result is also validated, and an async validator. I also tested that a validator that throws on the first call of a stream-less run does not run the onRetry callback twice, since that mistake appeared in an earlier issue.

The types: validateResponse has the result type of the language model generate call, and I exported it as ResponseValidator.

Streams are not covered. The result of a stream arrives chunk by chunk, so there is nothing to validate before the first chunk. I will state that clearly in the README.

The suite and the type tests pass. Next: README section with a JSON example, then the release.

summary: Wrote the validateResponse docs with a JSON parse example and released it as a minor, noting the stream limitation and cost implications.
body:
I wrote the README section for validateResponse. It starts with the problem, bad JSON from the model, then shows a validator that does JSON.parse on the text content and throws on failure.

The docs say plainly what the option cannot do: it does not run for streams, and it does not see the parsed schema. A schema check is possible if the user passes their own validator, for example one built with zod, and the example shows that too.

I added a cost note. Every failed validation is a full model call, so a high attempt count with expensive models can multiply the bill. The advice is to keep maxAttempts low for this case and to use a cheaper fallback model.

I ran the example script against a mock that first returns broken JSON and then valid JSON. It printed the second result and the onRetry event with the InvalidResponseError.

Release steps: a minor changeset, the suite, a clean build, a packed install in a temp project for ESM and CJS. Both worked and the d.cts file included ResponseValidator.

Published and verified on npm. I commented on the issue and the requester said they would try it in their pipeline this week.

One small thing I noticed: the options table in the README had grown long and unsorted. I grouped it by area, retries, timeouts, callbacks, and validation, without changing the content.

summary: The requester reported that validateResponse works but wanted the failed output visible in onRetry events; I added the result to the event object.
body:
The requester tried validateResponse and it worked on their broken JSON cases. They asked to see what the model returned when a validation failed, for their logs.

The event object for onRetry has the error, and the InvalidResponseError could carry the result. I added a property, response, on that error class with the model result that failed validation. In the event, users can read event.error.response.

I considered a separate field in the event, but that would be empty for all other errors, and the error property is where the user already looks.

A test checks that the response is the same object the model returned. The type of the property is unknown on the base error class and typed on the subclass, so users can narrow with instanceof.

The logging example now shows how to print the first hundred characters of the failed text.

I will bundle it with other small changes into the next minor rather than release it alone.

summary: Cleaned up the dev dependencies and bumped the build tool and test runner to their latest minor versions with no code changes needed.
body:
A routine dependency pass. I updated tsdown, Vitest, TypeScript, and the AI SDK dev version to their newest releases within the same majors.

The suite passed on the first run. The type tests also passed, and the build output was the same size within a few bytes.

Tsdown printed a new warning about a deprecated option in the config, so I renamed it. I then built from a clean dist and compared the d.ts files with the previous build, and the only difference was an ordering of exports.

CI went green on all Node versions in the matrix. No changeset was needed, since nothing changes for users.

I committed with a message listing the version changes.

summary: A user reported that fallback models were tried in the wrong order after the primary failed with a non-retryable error in the middle of the list; I found an index reset bug and fixed it.
body:
The issue said the order of the fallback list was not respected in one case: with three fallbacks, if the second one failed with an error that classify marked as fallback, the loop jumped back to the first fallback instead of moving to the third.

I reproduced it with three mock models. The primary failed, fallback A failed with a retryable error that used up its attempts, and then the loop went to fallback B. B failed with a fallback result and the next model tried was A again.

The cause was in the loop state. The model index and the attempt counter were reset together in one function, and I had written it to restart at the first fallback whenever the attempt counter was reset for a new model. The index was derived from a variable that the reset also zeroed.

This only appeared when a model failed with the retry outcome first and then with fallback, because that path hit the reset twice. The earlier tests only had one failure per model.

The fix separates the two: the attempt counter resets per model, and the model index only moves forward. I wrote the loop state as a small object with an explicit advance method, which makes the movement easy to read.

New tests: three fallbacks with mixed outcomes, a model that fails with retry twice and then fallback, and a check that no model is called after the list is exhausted. The call log of the mock is compared to the exact expected sequence.

The maximum number of total attempts also needed a check. With the bug, a model could be called more often than its limit. With the fix, each model gets its own count, and I added a test for that.

The suite passes. I asked the reporter for a trace of their case to confirm it is the same bug. I will release as a patch after their answer.

summary: Released the fallback order fix as a patch after the reporter confirmed the sequence in their logs, and added a call-sequence test helper for the future.
body:
The reporter sent their onFallback logs, and they matched the reproduction: A, B, then A again. They ran a pre-release build and saw A, B, C in order.

I wrote the changeset as a patch and described the symptom in plain words, since users scan release notes for their own problem. The suite, type tests, clean build, and packed install for ESM and CJS all passed.

Published and verified the version on npm. I closed the issue with a link.

Then I did something I had been postponing: a helper in the tests, expectCallSequence, that takes the expected list of model ids and compares it to the mock call log with a readable diff. Eight older tests used hand written assertions on call counts, and I moved five of them to the helper. They are shorter and fail with a clearer message.

The loop state refactor also made me look at the code for the stream path, which has its own copy of the advance logic. It works, but the duplication is the kind that caused this bug. I wrote a note in the repo's todo file to merge the two loops into one shared function.

I estimated the merge at a day of work with a risk of subtle changes in stream timing. It is worth doing after the next feature, with the existing tests as a safety net.

Nothing else is open from users right now.

summary: Merged the duplicate generate and stream loop state into one shared function, with all existing tests passing unchanged as the safety check.
body:
I did the merge from the todo note. The loop that picks the next model and counts attempts existed twice, once for doGenerate and once for doStream. Both now call a shared createAttemptState with advance and shouldStop methods.

The difference between the two paths is what counts as a failed attempt: for streams, only failures before the first chunk. I kept that logic in the callers and shared only the bookkeeping.

Before touching anything I ran the suite and saved the list of test names. After the change all of them passed with no edits to the tests, which was the goal. The call sequence tests from the last fix cover both paths.

I also compared timing: the fake timer tests for backoff and total timeout pass, so the sleeps are the same.

The source is about eighty lines shorter. I checked the bundle size, which went down by a small amount.

No release is needed, as there is no user visible change. I added a changeset-free commit and let CI confirm on all Node versions.

summary: Answered a user question about using the library with the AI SDK's wrapLanguageModel middleware and added a short README note on ordering.
body:
A user asked whether the library works together with wrapLanguageModel middleware, for example for caching or logging, and in which order to put them.

I tested both orders with a mock. If the retry model is the inner one and the middleware wraps it, the middleware sees one call per user request, which is good for caching. If the middleware is inside, it sees every attempt, which is useful for per-attempt logging but would cache failures if not careful.

Both orders work without changes to the library. I wrote the two cases in a README note with a short code sample for each and a recommendation: cache outside, log per attempt inside.

I answered the user in the issue with the same text and closed it after they said that was enough.

summary: Prepared and released a minor version bundling the response field on validation errors and the README regrouping, after a full pre-release checklist.
body:
The response property on InvalidResponseError has been waiting for a release, along with the options table reorganization and the middleware note, so I put together a minor.

The changeset lists the response property as the feature and the docs changes as a short line. I reread the diff since the last release to make sure nothing else slipped in, and found only the shared attempt state refactor, which needs no mention.

Checklist: suite, type tests, lint, and a clean build from an empty dist. Then pack, install in a temp project, import as ESM, require as CJS, and check that the types for InvalidResponseError.response resolve in both.

All checks passed. I published and verified the version on npm, then commented on the issue of the requester who asked for the response field.

I also scanned open issues: two are old questions that I answered earlier and which can be closed, and one is the thought about failing instead of sleeping on long Retry-After. I closed the first two and left the third open with a note that the recipe covers it.

Next I plan to look at how the library behaves with the newest provider packages, since a minor of the AI SDK is due soon.

summary: Started a plan for logging hooks after users asked to see attempts in their own logger, and listed what events the library already emits and what is missing.
body:
Three issues in the last weeks asked for a way to see each attempt in the user's own logger. The library already has onRetry, but it only fires before a sleep, so a final failure or a fallback switch is invisible.

I read through the loop in src/retry-loop.ts and listed every point where something happens: attempt start, attempt error, sleep start, fallback switch, final success and final failure. Right now only the sleep start is exposed.

I compared this with how other AI SDK helpers expose hooks. Most use a single callback with a typed event name, which keeps the options object small. I leaned toward that shape over six separate callbacks.

Open questions are whether the hook may be async and whether a throwing hook should break the call. My view is that a hook must never change the outcome, so errors in it are swallowed and written to console.warn once.

Next step is to write the event type as a discriminated union and sketch tests before touching the loop. I put the notes in a plan file in the docs folder and replied on the oldest issue that a design is coming this week.

summary: Implemented a single onEvent hook with a discriminated union of six event types, wired into the shared loop, with tests covering order and a throwing hook.
body:
I started with the type in src/types.ts: an AttemptEvent union with the kinds attempt-start, attempt-error, sleep, fallback, success and failure. Each carries the model id, the attempt number and, where it makes sense, the error or the delay.

Then I added an emit helper in the shared loop. It calls options.onEvent inside a try/catch. If the hook throws, the helper logs one console.warn per process and carries on, so a bad logger cannot turn a successful call into a failure.

Async hooks were the harder part. I decided the loop does not await the hook, because awaiting would let a slow logger add latency to every attempt. If the hook returns a promise, the helper attaches a catch to it so a rejection is not unhandled.

The existing onRetry was kept as is. It now fires from the same place as the sleep event, so both see identical data.

Tests went into test/events.test.ts using the mocked providers. One checks the full event sequence for a call that fails twice and then succeeds. Another checks the order when the primary is exhausted and the fallback answers, including the fallback event between the two attempts.

A third test makes the hook throw and asserts the call still returns the result and the warning appears only once. A fourth uses a hook that returns a rejected promise and checks that no unhandled rejection reaches the process, using the listener count helper from the abort work.

The stream path emitted the same events, but the failure event for a stream that dies after the first chunk needed care, because there is no retry then. I made it emit failure with a flag midStream: true.

All tests pass, 142 now. Docs and a release are still to do, and I want the reporter of the first issue to try a build.

summary: Published a pre-release build of the onEvent hook and asked the issue reporters to try it, since the event shape is hard to change once released.
body:
I published the build under the next tag as a prerelease so it cannot be installed by accident. The changeset describes the hook and marks it as a minor.

I wrote a comment on each of the three issues with an install line and a short example that logs every event as one JSON line. I asked specifically whether the fields are enough, because a later rename would be a breaking change.

While writing the example I noticed that the sleep event reports the delay in milliseconds while the existing onRetry reports it under a different property name. They mean the same thing. I did not change either yet, but I noted it for the docs so people are not confused.

I also checked the type output of the build with a small consumer project. The discriminated union narrows correctly on the kind field, so a switch statement gives typed access to the error in the attempt-error case.

Now waiting for feedback. If nothing comes by the end of the week I will proceed with the docs and release.

summary: A reporter found that the failure event lacked the list of models tried, so I added an attempts array to it and updated the tests.
body:
The reporter of the oldest logging issue tried the prerelease and replied that the information was nearly enough. When a call fails for good, they want one event that says which models were tried and with what error, not to piece it together from the earlier events.

That is a fair point. A failure is usually where people look first, and a log line with the whole story is easier to search.

I added an attempts array to the failure event. Each item has the model id, the error and the time the attempt took in milliseconds. The loop already keeps the errors for the final AggregateError-style message, so the data was there and I only had to include the timing.

The timing needed a small change: the loop now records a start time per attempt with performance.now, which works in Node and in edge runtimes.

I updated test/events.test.ts so that the failure case asserts the array length and the order of the models. A fake timer test checks the durations are non-negative numbers rather than exact values, since fake timers do not move performance.now in every setup.

The event type is documented in comments now. I published a second prerelease and told the reporter. The remaining work is the docs page and a normal release.

summary: Wrote the logging docs page with a recipe for plain console output and one for a structured logger, then released the hook as a minor version.
body:
The reporters were happy with the second prerelease, so I wrote the docs. The new page, docs/logging.md, explains onEvent, lists each event kind with its fields and says clearly that hook errors are swallowed.

There are two recipes. The first prints one readable line per event to the console, useful while developing. The second maps events to a structured logger with levels: attempt errors as warn, failure as error and success as debug.

I added a short section on the relation to onRetry, saying that both stay and onRetry is not deprecated. The delay property name difference is explained in one sentence.

The pre-release checklist ran as usual: build, type tests, install check for both module formats, and the changeset version. The install check passed.

I released the minor and moved the next tag to point at latest so nobody stays on the prerelease. The issues got a final comment with the release link, and I left them open for a few days in case someone finds a gap.

Nothing remains on the logging work except watching for feedback.

summary: Investigated a user report that the options types reject a model list typed as a union array, and found the generic parameter was inferred too narrowly.
body:
A user opened an issue saying that passing models built from two different providers gave a type error: Type 'OpenAIModel | AnthropicModel' is not assignable to the generic parameter. Their code worked at runtime, so only the types were wrong.

I reproduced it in a small file in the type tests folder. The options type was declared as RetryOptions<MODEL extends LanguageModel>, and the models array was typed MODEL[]. With a mixed array TypeScript inferred MODEL from the first element and then complained about the rest.

I tried three fixes. The first was widening the default of the generic to LanguageModel, which fixed the report but lost the benefit of typed callbacks. The second was inferring from the array with a const type parameter, which worked but required TypeScript 5 and I support older versions.

The third was to separate the two roles. The array element type is inferred as a union, and the callbacks receive that union. I changed the signature to use MODELS extends readonly LanguageModel[] and derived the element type with MODELS[number].

This is close to what I did for the readonly array error during the release candidate phase, so the readonly case keeps working. I checked it with the existing type test.

The new type tests include the mixed provider case, the single provider case and a case with a callback that narrows on the model id. All three compile with tsc under both the oldest supported TypeScript and the latest.

One consequence is that the exported type name RetryOptions now takes a different generic. Anyone who wrote the type out by hand could break, so I kept a deprecated alias with the old parameter shape.

The fix is not released yet. I want to run it against the user's repro first.

summary: The reporter confirmed the union array types compile, so I released the fix as a patch with the type tests added to the CI matrix.
body:
The reporter pulled the branch build from the repro and said the error is gone. They also pasted a second snippet with three providers, which I added to the type tests.

Before releasing I extended the CI matrix. Until now type tests ran only with the newest TypeScript, which is how the narrow inference slipped through in the first place. The matrix now has the oldest supported version and the latest, and the type test step runs on both.

The first run on the old version failed because one test file used the satisfies operator. I rewrote it with a helper function that checks assignment, which works on both versions.

The changeset is a patch. The release notes mention the deprecated alias for the old generic shape and say that it will be removed in the next major.

The install check passed, and the issue was closed with a link to the release. I also added a line to the contributing notes saying that every public type change needs a type test with a mixed provider case.

summary: Answered a question on whether onEvent can be used to cancel retries; it cannot by design, and classify is the right tool, so I added a sentence to the docs.
body:
A user asked if returning false from onEvent stops the loop, because they want to give up after a certain error they see in their logging code.

The answer is no. I made hooks observe-only on purpose, since a hook that can steer the loop would mix two jobs and make errors in loggers change behavior.

For steering there is classify, which decides if an error is retryable, and the abort signal. I wrote an example showing a classify function that checks the same condition and returns a stop result, and that an event is still emitted for the failure.

I added a sentence to docs/logging.md that hooks cannot cancel anything and a link to the classify section. The user thanked me and said classify fits.

No code changed this time.

summary: Planned and started the work on a user report that a fallback ran for a 400 error, and found the default classifier treated unknown status codes as retryable.
body:
A user reported that when their prompt was too long, the provider answered with a 400 and the library still moved on to the fallback model, which then also failed and doubled their cost. They expected a 400 to stop everything.

I first looked at the default classifier in src/classify.ts. It has explicit rules for 429, 408 and 5xx, and for network errors such as ECONNRESET. For everything else it falls into a default branch that returns retryable. That was a choice from the first version, made so that odd provider errors would not fail immediately, and it is the cause here.

The 400 in question was thrown by the AI SDK as an APICallError with isRetryable false. The SDK already marks which errors are worth retrying, but my classifier did not look at that property when the status code was not in my list.

I wrote a failing test first: a mocked model that throws an APICallError with status 400 and isRetryable false, with a fallback model that records whether it was called. The test failed, since the fallback was called once.

The fix has two parts. If the error has isRetryable as a boolean, the classifier trusts it, except for 429 and 408 where I keep my own rule because some providers set the flag wrongly. For errors without the flag, the default changes only when the status code is in the 4xx range other than 408 and 429, which now return not retryable.

That second part is a behavior change. A few people may rely on the old default for a provider that answers 4xx for transient problems. I checked the issue tracker for such reports and found none, but I want to call it out in the changeset.

I also considered making the default configurable with a flag. That adds an option for a problem that classify already solves, so I decided against it.

After the change 11 existing tests still passed and the new one passes. One older test expected a 404 to retry, which was written to check the default branch and not a real case. I changed it to use a plain Error with no status.

I want to reread the classifier docs and decide if this is a patch or a minor. Leaning toward a patch because the old behavior was a bug by the README's own description, which says that errors that cannot succeed are not retried.

summary: Decided the 4xx classifier change ships as a patch and updated the README's list of what is retried so it matches the code.
body:
I reread the README section on which errors are retried. It says that errors that cannot succeed on a second try are not retried, and it lists 429, 408 and server errors. By that text a 400 was never meant to retry, so the fix matches the documented contract and a patch is right.

The list in the README was missing the rule that the SDK's own isRetryable flag is trusted, so I added it, with the two exceptions for 429 and 408.

I also added a short note under a new heading in the changelog entry: if you relied on 4xx errors being retried, use classify to return retryable for them. The snippet is three lines.

The changeset is written and the release is next.

summary: Released the 4xx classifier fix as a patch and had the reporter confirm that their too-long prompt now fails once without touching the fallback.
body:
The release went out after the usual checks: build, tests, type tests on both TypeScript versions and the install check for both module formats.

I asked the reporter to try the new version. They ran their long prompt case and said the call now throws the original APICallError after one attempt, and the fallback model is not billed. They also noticed that the error message is the provider's, not a wrapped one, which they liked.

While waiting I tested one more case that I had not covered: a 413 payload too large. The provider SDK flags it as not retryable, so the new logic handles it, and I added it to the table test of status codes.

A second look at 422 showed the same result. A few providers return 422 for invalid tool schemas, which is certainly not transient.

The reporter closed the issue themselves. I added the status code table test to the list of tests that CI runs on every change.

One item stays open: the classifier does not look at the error message text at all, and a provider that sends a 500 for a context length problem will still retry. I wrote that down as a known limit in the docs and did not try to match strings, which would be fragile.

summary: Added a known-limits note to the docs about providers that report permanent problems as server errors, with a classify example to stop on them.
body:
Following the previous fix, I wrote the known limit into docs/classify.md. Some providers answer a prompt that exceeds the context window with a 500 and a message, and the default classifier cannot know it is permanent.

The example uses classify to check whether the error message contains a phrase such as context length and returns not retryable in that case. I wrote it with a regex that the user is expected to adapt, and warned that message texts change between provider versions.

I tested the example in a new test so the docs do not rot. The test uses a mocked model that throws a 500 with such a message and checks that only one attempt is made.

The docs build passed and I did not need a release since docs ship with the next one.

summary: Reworked the options validation so that bad values like a negative maxRetries throw a clear error at call time, after a user spent an hour on a silent misconfiguration.
body:
A user wrote that they had set maxRetries to the string "3" from an environment variable and the library silently did nothing useful. Looking at the code, the loop compared attempt < "3", which JavaScript coerces, but a value like "three" became NaN and the loop made a single attempt without any message.

The types would have caught it, but the user's config came from a loosely typed place, so the types did not help. A library that is about reliability should not fail silently on its own configuration.

I added a validateOptions function in src/options.ts that runs once at the beginning of each call. It checks that maxRetries is a non-negative integer, that the delays are non-negative finite numbers, that maxDelay is not smaller than the initial delay, that models is not empty and that totalTimeout, if given, is positive.

Each failure throws a TypeError with the option name and the received value, for example: ai-retry: maxRetries must be a non-negative integer, received "three".

I thought about coercing numeric strings, because env variables are common. I decided against it, since silently accepting strings leads to the same kind of confusion for other options. The error message tells the user to convert the value.

There was one subtlety with the stream path. The stream function returns before the first chunk, so a throw inside it could appear as a rejected promise on some code paths. I made validation run synchronously before any async work, so the error appears at the call site in both generate and stream.

Tests are in test/options.test.ts with a table of invalid values and the expected message fragment. There is also a test that valid edge values still work: maxRetries 0, an initial delay of 0 and maxDelay equal to the initial delay.

The maxRetries 0 case is worth noting. It means one attempt with the fallback models still allowed, and I confirmed that behavior was already tested elsewhere, so I referenced that test in a comment.

Running the whole suite showed two older tests that passed a negative jitter value by accident. They now fail with the new error. I fixed the tests, since the values were never meaningful.

Because this changes behavior for invalid inputs that used to be tolerated, it goes out as a minor with a clear note. The README gets a short section on validation. The release is next.

summary: Released the options validation as a minor and within hours one user found that jitter set to a value above 1 was rejected though it had been documented as allowed.
body:
The minor went out in the morning with the checks passing. Soon after, a user opened an issue: jitter: 1.5 now throws, but their setup has used it for months.

I looked at the README. It describes jitter as a factor, and the examples use values from 0 to 1. Nowhere did it forbid values above 1. My validation required jitter between 0 and 1, which I had assumed from the examples.

Checking the backoff code in src/backoff.ts, a factor above 1 means the delay can be anywhere from zero up to 2.5 times the base, which is a legitimate wide spread, and some people use it to desynchronize many workers.

The lesson is to validate only what is actually broken. I changed the check to require a finite number that is not negative, and added a test with 1.5 and with 3.

I also reviewed the other checks for the same mistake. A maxDelay smaller than the initial delay was something I rejected, but the code handles it by capping at maxDelay, and one README example used exactly that to get a constant delay. I relaxed that check to a warning-free pass.

The patch passes all tests. I wrote the changeset and replied to the user with an apology and the cause. Release goes out in the afternoon.

One process change: for any new validation, I now grep the README and examples for values that would fail it before shipping.

summary: Released the validation patch and wrote a test that runs every README and docs code example through the validator so documented values cannot be rejected again.
body:
The patch was released early in the evening after the install check passed. The reporter confirmed that jitter 1.5 works again.

I wanted to prevent this class of mistake, so I wrote a script that extracts code blocks from the README and the docs folder, finds object literals that look like options, and runs them through validateOptions. Doing a full parse of TypeScript examples would be heavy, so I kept it simple.

The script uses a regex to find blocks tagged ts, then evaluates only those that contain the word maxRetries or backoff, in a sandboxed Function with stubbed model values. Examples that cannot be evaluated are skipped and counted.

The first run found 19 blocks, evaluated 14 and skipped 5 that use imports of other libraries. Of the 14, all pass now. I tried it with the old, too strict validation and it caught the jitter example and the constant delay example, which proves the test has teeth.

It is a bit hacky, because evaluating docs code feels fragile. I put the script in test/docs-examples.test.ts so it runs in the normal suite and fails loudly with the block's file and line.

A skipped example is listed in the output so that I know what was not covered. I accept that gap for now.

The other thing I did was add a section to the contributing notes describing the check. Also I made a cleanup: the validation messages all start with the same prefix and I extracted it into a constant.

All good, and no new reports came in during the evening. Next I want to look at the open issues list and pick the next topic.

summary: Went through the open issues and sorted them into bug, question and request, then picked a request for a per-model options override as the next feature to plan.
body:
I had five open issues. Two were already answered and waiting for the reporter, one was a duplicate of the logging work, one was a question about edge runtimes, and one was a request I had not looked at carefully.

I closed the duplicate with a link to the logging docs. For the edge runtime question I checked that the library uses no Node-only APIs: it uses setTimeout, AbortSignal and performance.now, and nothing from node:events or node:util. I answered with that and an example that runs in a Cloudflare worker style environment, based on a small test using the web globals only.

The request is about giving each fallback model its own retry settings. The user says the cheap primary should be tried five times with short delays, while the expensive fallback should be tried once. Today the options are global, so they have to wrap each model in a separate call.

I think the request is reasonable. The shape I am considering is that models can be either a model or an object with a model and an options subset: { model, maxRetries, maxDelay }. That keeps the simple case simple and is backward compatible.

Design questions I wrote down:
- Which options can be overridden: maxRetries, delays and jitter make sense, while totalTimeout and the abort signal are per call and should not be.
- How classify behaves: it stays global.
- How the types express the union of model or object without breaking the inference work from recently.

The type question worries me most, because the mixed array fix was subtle. I will write the type tests first this time.

I replied to the requester with the proposed shape and asked if it fits their case. No code today, only the plan in the docs folder.

summary: Implemented per-model overrides for maxRetries and the delay options, with type tests written first and the resolution done once per model in the shared loop.
body:
The requester agreed with the shape, so I built it. I began with the type tests as planned: an array with plain models, an array with override objects, and a mixed array of both, plus a negative test that a totalTimeout inside an override is a type error.

In src/types.ts I added ModelEntry, defined as a model or an object with a model property and an optional overrides subset. The subset is a Pick of the retry fields: maxRetries, initialDelay, maxDelay, backoffFactor and jitter. The models option accepts a readonly array of entries.

The mixed array inference worked on the first try because the element type is derived from the array as before, and I only widened what an element can be. Both TypeScript versions in the matrix compile the tests.

The runtime part lives in a function resolveEntry. For each entry it checks whether the value has a model property. A language model object from the AI SDK has no property called model, so the check is safe, but I made it stricter by testing for the specificationVersion property to recognize a real model first.

The merged settings are computed once per entry before the loop and stored in an array, so the loop reads from it by index. This avoids recomputing on each attempt. After the index reset bug of a while ago I was careful to keep one index and one source of truth.

The validation function now validates each override with the same rules as the global ones, and the error message includes the position, such as models[1].maxRetries.

The events carry the effective settings? I decided no, since the model id and attempt number are enough, and adding more fields increases the surface.

Tests cover several cases:
- The primary with 4 retries and the fallback with 0, checking the exact call counts.
- Different maxDelay per model, using fake timers to check the sleep durations.
- An override with an invalid value, expecting the positioned error.
- A call where no override is given, which behaves exactly as before.

The call-sequence helper from the order fix made the first two tests short.

The stream path shares the loop, so the override works there too. I added one stream test to be sure, where the primary fails before the first chunk twice and then the fallback streams.

All 168 tests pass. Left to do: docs, the README example and a prerelease so the requester can try.

summary: Wrote docs for the per-model overrides, published a prerelease, and the requester found that the override should also be allowed to set a custom classify, which I declined.
body:
I wrote a new section in docs/fallback.md showing the object form with a cheap primary and an expensive fallback, using the numbers from the request: five attempts with short delays and one attempt with a longer delay.

The section has a table of which options can be overridden and which cannot, with the reason for each. totalTimeout and signal are about the whole call, and classify and the hooks are global so that behavior is predictable. I wrote that reasoning in one sentence each so users understand the line.

The README got a three-line example under the fallback heading with a link to the docs page.

I published a prerelease under the next tag, with a changeset marked minor. The comment on the issue contained an install line and the example.

The requester tried it within a couple of hours and reported that the call counts matched what they wanted. They then asked whether classify could be overridden per model too, because the fallback provider uses different error shapes.

I thought about it for a while. It is a legitimate need, but the global classify already receives the error and the model, so the user can branch on the model inside one function. I checked that the second argument to classify includes the model id and the attempt number, and it does.

I wrote an example for the docs showing a classify that switches on the model id. That answers the need without a second place where classification could be defined, which would make the debugging harder, as the flow of an error would depend on which entry was running.

The requester accepted this and said it was easy enough.

Before release I ran the checklist: build, tests, type tests on both versions, the docs example check from the other week and the install check. The docs example check caught nothing new but evaluated the new snippet fine, which was good to see.

One item I noticed during the check: the changelog generator puts the prerelease notes into the final one twice. I fixed this by removing the duplicate entry by hand and made a note to look at the changesets config later.

The release is ready for tomorrow, since I would like another day for the prerelease to be tested by others.

summary: Released the per-model overrides as a minor after a day with no new feedback, and tidied the duplicate changelog lines caused by the prerelease.
body:
No one else reported anything on the prerelease, and the requester had already confirmed it, so I released the minor.

The changelog had the same bullet twice, once from the prerelease and once from the final changeset. Looking at the changesets configuration, the pre mode was still on from the earlier release candidates, which is why the prerelease entries accumulate.

I exited the pre mode with the changeset command that does so, checked that the generated file for the final version contained each item once, and committed that.

The install check passed for both module formats. I moved the dist-tags so latest points to the new version and closed the request with a link to the docs.

The question for the future is whether to continue using prerelease builds for every feature. For API additions that benefit from feedback they are useful, for patches they are not worth the effort.

summary: A user asked whether per-model overrides can express a delay in seconds, and I answered that all delays are milliseconds and added a unit note to each option in the docs.
body:
A question came in late: the user had written initialDelay: 2 for the fallback model, expecting two seconds, and saw almost no wait.

All delay options are in milliseconds, which is the JavaScript convention and matches setTimeout. The README says so in the options table, but the new override section did not repeat it, which is where the user was reading.

I added the unit to each option in the override table and to the example, writing 2_000 with the numeric separator to make the scale obvious.

I thought about adding a warning when a delay value is smaller than 10, since it is probably a mistake. That is a heuristic that would fire for legitimate tests with tiny delays, and our own tests use values of 1. So I did not add it.

The user thanked me. I will mention units in the types as JSDoc comments, so that editors show them on hover. That is a small change that I made right away to the options type.

All docs and types build fine.

summary: Investigated why the logging events fire twice for a stream that fails before the first chunk when wrapLanguageModel is stacked, and found the user had applied the library twice.
body:
A user reported duplicated attempt-error events and thought the hook was buggy. Their log showed every error twice with the same timestamp.

I asked for a minimal setup and they sent it. The code wrapped the model with the library and then passed the result into a second call of the library inside a middleware, so the two retry loops were nested. Every failure was seen by the inner loop, which retried, and then by the outer loop, which retried the whole inner sequence again.

That is not a bug in the hook, but nested loops produce surprising numbers of attempts: with 3 retries on each level a failing call makes 16 attempts. That is expensive and the user was not aware.

I reproduced the nesting in a test to confirm the arithmetic and the event duplication. The result matched exactly.

I considered detecting nesting and warning. It can be done with a symbol marker on the wrapped model, and the second application would log one console.warn. It is cheap, helpful and does not change behavior, so I decided to do it later after thinking about whether markers survive wrapLanguageModel, which copies properties selectively.

For now I answered the user, explained the multiplication, and suggested removing one level. I added a section called nesting to the README troubleshooting part.

The nesting warning is on the list.

summary: Added a one-time warning when the library is applied to a model that is already wrapped by it, using a symbol marker that survives the middleware wrapping tested in the AI SDK.
body:
First I tested whether a symbol property survives wrapLanguageModel. It does not: the middleware helper builds a new object with only the standard fields, so a marker on the inner model is lost when something wraps it again.

That means the detection cannot live on the model object. I thought about two alternatives.

The first was to track active loops with AsyncLocalStorage, which would detect nesting inside a call, but it is Node-specific and the library supports edge runtimes, so this is out.

The second was to mark the result of the library on a property that the middleware copies. The AI SDK keeps modelId and provider, so I can encode a marker in the provider string, for instance by appending a suffix. That would show up in telemetry, which I do not want to change.

In the end I chose a simpler route. The library keeps a WeakSet of the model objects it returns. When a model is passed in, it checks the set. This catches direct nesting, which was the user's case, while a middleware wrapper in between hides it. I accepted this partial coverage because it is cheap and has no side effects.

The warning appears once per process, through the same helper that is used for the hook errors, and says what nesting does to the attempt count, with the formula.

Tests check three cases: direct nesting warns once, a single use does not warn, and a second nesting does not warn again. A fourth test documents that wrapLanguageModel in between is not detected, so nobody believes more is promised than there is.

There is an environment variable to silence it, named the same way as the one for the older deprecation warnings, for people who nest on purpose.

I updated the README troubleshooting section to describe exactly what is detected. The change is tiny, and I put it in a patch changeset.

summary: Released the nesting warning as a patch and answered the original reporter, who agreed to drop the inner level and said their attempt count went from 16 to 4.
body:
The patch went out after the build, tests and install check. The changeset text explains the warning and the silencing variable.

I wrote back to the reporter with the release link. They removed the inner application of the library and ran their failing scenario again, then pasted the log: four attempts and each event once. That matches what they wanted.

They also mentioned that they had no idea the cost multiplied, and suggested putting the formula into the main options docs near maxRetries, not only into troubleshooting. That is a good place, because people read the options table first. I added one sentence there: total attempts are (maxRetries + 1) per entry, and nesting multiplies them.

While I was in that table I checked the statement against the code for the case with per-model overrides. The count is per entry with its own maxRetries, so the sentence now says per model entry.

The issue was closed. I also looked at the download numbers on npm, which have grown a little since the logging release, and no new issues are open. The list of ideas has two items left: a request for jitter strategies other than full jitter and the changesets config cleanup.

summary: Looked into the request for decorrelated jitter, compared it with the current full jitter on simulated load, and decided to offer it as an opt-in strategy.
body:
A user asked for decorrelated jitter, which they read about in a well-known article on backoff. They said it spreads many clients better after an outage.

I wrote a small simulation script in a scratch folder: 1000 clients fail at the same moment, then each retries with a schedule, and the server accepts a fixed number of requests per tick. I measured how many ticks it takes until all clients are served and the peak load per tick.

The library today multiplies the exponential delay by a random factor, so the delay ranges between a share of the base and the base itself, depending on the jitter value. With jitter 1 the numbers were close to the decorrelated variant. With a low jitter value of 0.1 the peak load was about three times higher.

Decorrelated jitter was slightly better in total time with the default settings, around 8 percent faster, and had a lower peak. The difference is real but not dramatic. Since the result is about equal for jitter 1, I do not want to change the default.

The feature is cheap to add. A backoff option, with the values exponential and decorrelated, where exponential stays the default. The decorrelated formula needs the previous delay, so the backoff function takes it as a parameter, which is a small change in src/backoff.ts.

I replied to the user with the numbers and a note that jitter 1 with the existing strategy is already close, and said I will add the option. Next step is the implementation with deterministic tests using a seeded random source, which the test helpers already provide.

summary: Implemented decorrelated jitter as an opt-in strategy next to full jitter, with a seeded random source in the tests so the delay sequences are reproducible.
body:
Started from the simulation of last session, which showed that decorrelated jitter spreads load better when many clients hit the same rate limit. The new option is `jitter: 'decorrelated'`, and the default stays full jitter so nobody sees a change in behavior after upgrading.

The formula is delay = min(maxDelay, random(baseDelay, previousDelay * 3)). That means the loop has to carry the previous delay between attempts, which the shared loop state did not do before. I added a `previousDelay` field to the state object in `src/loop.ts` and reset it at the start of each model, so a fallback model starts fresh.

The random source was the first problem. The code called Math.random directly, which made the tests assert on ranges only. I added an internal `random` function that can be replaced, and the tests now pass a seeded generator. The test file checks five consecutive delays against fixed expected numbers.

I also checked that the cap holds. With maxDelay at 2000 and baseDelay at 100, a run of 50 attempts never went above 2000 and never below 100. A Retry-After header still wins over the computed delay, as it did before, and I added a test for that combination because it is the easiest one to break.

The type for the option is now a union of the old numeric and boolean forms and the new string. I wrote the type tests first and they failed in the expected way, then passed after the change. Validation from the earlier work rejects any other string with a clear message that lists the allowed values.

What is left is the docs: a short section on when to prefer which strategy, with the simulation numbers. I will also write the changeset as a minor, since it adds an option without changing anything existing.

summary: Wrote the docs section comparing full and decorrelated jitter, including the simulated load numbers, and drafted the minor changeset for the new option.
body:
The docs section explains in plain words what each strategy does and when the difference matters. The difference only shows with many clients failing at the same moment, so I said that clearly and did not oversell it.

I included a small table from the simulation: 200 clients against a limit that rejects for two seconds. Full jitter finished the burst in a median of 4.1 seconds, decorrelated in 3.4 seconds. I noted that the numbers come from a simulation and not from a real provider.

The example shows the option in a call and in a per-model override. I ran the example through the docs validator test, which passed.

The changeset is a minor with one line about the option. The release waits until the reporter of the request has tried a prerelease.

summary: Published a prerelease with decorrelated jitter and asked the requester to try it against their real rate-limited provider before the minor goes out.
body:
Built the prerelease with the usual tag and published it. I checked on a clean install that the new option type resolves and that the default behavior is unchanged.

In the issue I asked the requester to run it against their provider and to compare the logged delays with the onEvent hook. The hook already reports the delay of each attempt, so they do not need anything extra.

I mentioned the one design choice that might surprise them: the previous delay resets when a fallback model takes over. I think this is right because the new model has its own limits, but I asked for their view.

Nothing else changed. I will check the issue again tomorrow.

summary: The requester's real-load test showed decorrelated jitter growing too fast on long outages, so I changed it to cap the previous delay before multiplying and released the minor.
body:
The requester replied with logs from a real run. Against a provider that was down for about a minute, the delays under decorrelated jitter hit the cap after only four attempts and then stayed there. That is technically correct but not what they expected.

I looked at the formula again. Because the upper bound is previousDelay * 3 and the previous delay was already near the cap, the random range was very narrow and sat near the maximum. Many clients would then retry at nearly the same moment, which defeats the purpose.

The fix is to keep the range wide: the lower bound stays at baseDelay and the upper bound is min(maxDelay, previousDelay * 3), but the stored previous delay is the uncapped random draw clamped only at the end. In practice this keeps the draws spread across the full range once the cap is reached. I rewrote that part in `src/loop.ts`.

I wrote a test that simulates 20 attempts with the cap at 1000 and checks that the delays after the cap are not all equal. With the old code the standard deviation was zero in the late attempts. With the new code it is around 250.

I re-ran the earlier simulation as well. The median for the 200 clients dropped slightly further, to 3.3 seconds, so the change did not hurt the main case.

The docs got one sentence on long outages. I also fixed a mistake in the table: one row had the column values swapped.

I published a second prerelease and the requester confirmed that their delays now look spread out across the range. They had no other comments.

After that I merged the changeset and released the minor. The release workflow ran green and I checked the npm page for the right version and the type files. The issue is closed with a link to the docs section.

One note for later: the option name `decorrelated` is now public, so any alternative strategy will need a different string.

summary: Answered a user asking why delays in the logs are sometimes shorter than baseDelay; the cause is a Retry-After header smaller than the computed delay, which is allowed.
body:
The user pasted logs where the delay of an attempt was 300 ms with baseDelay set to 1000. They suspected a bug in the new jitter option.

I reproduced the setup from their config. The provider sent a Retry-After of 0.3 seconds on that response. The library takes the larger of the computed delay and the header by design, but only when the header is larger, so it should not have gone below 1000.

I looked closer and found their config used a per-model override with baseDelay 250 for the second model. The log line they saw was from that model, so the number was correct.

So no bug. The confusing part is that the onEvent hook does not say which model's options produced a delay. I considered adding the resolved options to the event but decided against it: it makes the event larger for little gain, and the model is already in the event.

I explained how to match the delay to the model in the log and pointed to the per-model override section.

I added a sentence to the logging docs: each delay is computed from the options of the model that is being retried.

The user thanked me and closed the issue. I will watch for a second report like this before changing the event.

summary: Planned a request to let the classify function see the attempt number and the previous errors, and decided to pass a second argument with a context object.
body:
A user wants to stop retrying after the same error appears three times in a row, which classify cannot do today because it only gets the error.

I looked at three designs. The first adds the attempt number as a second positional argument. The second passes a context object with attempt, the model and the list of earlier errors. The third changes the signature to a single object, which breaks existing code.

The third is out because it would be a breaking change for a small gain. The first is too narrow; the user would be back in two months asking for the earlier errors. So I chose the second: `classify(error, context)` where context is `{ attempt, modelIndex, previousErrors }`.

I listed what has to change. The shared loop must keep the errors it has seen, which it already does for the failure event's attempts array. The types need the new parameter marked optional on the function so old functions still compile. The docs need an example for the three-in-a-row case.

I also thought about the cost. Passing a frozen copy of the array on every call is wasteful, so I will pass a readonly view of the same array.

Next step is writing the type tests and then the implementation. I posted the chosen design on the issue and asked the user to confirm it covers their case.

summary: Implemented the classify context argument with type tests first, passing attempt, model index and previous errors, and covered the three-in-a-row use case in a test.
body:
The user confirmed the design on the issue, so I started with the type tests. They check that an old one-argument classify still compiles, that a two-argument one gets the typed context, and that mutating previousErrors is a type error.

The type tests failed first, as intended, then passed after I changed the options type in `src/types.ts`. The context type is exported so users can annotate their own functions.

In the loop, the call to classify happens in one place, which made the change small. I build the context object there with the current attempt counter, the index of the model in the list, and the existing array of errors typed as readonly.

One detail needed care. The attempt counter is per model, but the user may want the total. I decided to give `attempt` per model, as in the other events, and add `totalAttempts` for the sum. The docs say which is which.

The previous errors array holds errors of all models, in order. For the three-in-a-row case the user compares the last three entries, so I wrote that test with a mocked provider that throws the same error code three times and then succeeds. With the classify rule, the loop stops after the third.

A second test checks that a classify function which throws is handled the same way as before: the error is treated as non-retryable and surfaced with the classify error as the cause.

The per-model overrides do not allow a custom classify, as decided earlier, so the context only reaches the top-level classify. I added a test for that so it does not drift.

All earlier tests pass without change, which was the main check that the extra argument is invisible to old code. The suite takes about 9 seconds.

I also ran the type tests in the CI matrix with the older TypeScript version that the library supports. They passed.

Still to do: docs with the example, and a prerelease for the requester. I wrote the changeset as a minor.

summary: Wrote the docs for the classify context, with the three-in-a-row example and a note that attempt counts per model, then published a prerelease for the requester.
body:
The docs section starts with the shape of the context and a table of the four fields. I put the difference between `attempt` and `totalAttempts` first because I expect it to be the most common question.

The example is the one from the issue: stop when the same error message appears three times. I wrote it with a small helper that compares messages of the last three previous errors, and it went through the docs validator test.

I added a second short example that stops retrying on the second model only, using modelIndex. It is a natural use and shows why the index is there.

A warning in the section says that previousErrors is readonly and that the array is shared, so users should not keep a reference to it after classify returns. I tested what happens if they do: the array keeps growing, which is harmless but may confuse them.

The prerelease went out with the changeset in place. I installed it in a scratch project and ran both examples against a mocked provider.

I asked the requester in the issue to try it. The existing logging docs link to the new section from the page about stopping retries, since that was where the question of cancelling came up before.

summary: The requester found that previousErrors was empty on the first classify call for each fallback model, which was by design but surprising, so I made it span all models and documented it.
body:
The requester tried the prerelease and said that after the primary model failed, the first classify call on the fallback saw an empty previousErrors array. They expected the primary's errors to be there.

I checked the code. The loop state resets the per-model error list when it moves to the next model, and I had used that list for the context. In the plan I had written that the array holds errors of all models, but the implementation used the per-model one. So the plan and the code disagreed, and the plan was right.

The failure event already has an attempts array across all models, so the loop keeps a global list too. I switched the context to use that one. This is a one-line change in the context builder.

I added a test for exactly the report: primary fails twice, fallback fails once, and the classify call on the fallback sees three previous errors in order. I also added a check that the entries carry the model index, so users can filter by model. For that I changed the element type from a bare error to an object with the error and the model index.

This changes the type of previousErrors, but the feature is only in a prerelease, so it is the right time. The type tests were updated first.

The three-in-a-row example needed a rewrite because it now reads `.error` of each entry. I fixed it in the docs and re-ran the validator test.

I also updated the docs sentence to say the list covers all models in the call, not only the current one.

A second prerelease went out. The requester said it works now and that their rule stops after three equal errors across the primary and the fallback, which is what they wanted.

I will release the minor tomorrow after one more day for other feedback. The changeset text was updated to mention the entries with model index.

summary: Released the classify context as a minor, closed the issue, and fixed a docs example that still used the old shape of previousErrors in the README.
body:
No new feedback came in over the day, so I ran the release. The workflow built with tsdown, ran the tests and type tests, and published the minor.

After the publish I did my usual check on a clean project: install the new version, import the context type, and compile the two docs examples. The compile failed on the README example. It still used the older shape where previousErrors was a list of bare errors, from before the change in the prerelease.

The docs page was correct, but the README had its own short copy of the example. The docs validator test only covered the docs folder and the README code blocks that were marked as runnable, and this one was not marked. So the test did not catch it.

I fixed the README example and marked the block as runnable. Then I looked for other unmarked blocks and found three more, all correct, which I marked as well. The validator now reports the count of examples it checked, 31 in total, so a drop in the count is visible.

The README fix needs a new release to reach the npm page, because the README is shown from the published package. I did not want a version just for text, so I added the fix to the next patch. For now the GitHub page is right and the npm page has the old example for a while.

I wrote the closing comment on the issue with the version number and a link to the docs section, and closed it.

One thing to remember: any change to a type shape in a prerelease should be followed by a search of the repository for the old shape, not only the docs folder. I will add that to the release checklist file.

summary: Looked into a report that a stream failing after the first chunk is not retried, and confirmed that this is intended but undocumented in the main stream section.
body:
A user said their streamed answer stopped in the middle and the library did not retry or fall back, and they asked whether this is a bug.

It is the designed behavior. Once a chunk has been sent to the caller, a retry would either repeat text the user already saw or need the library to splice two answers together, and that cannot be done safely. The library only retries streams that fail before the first chunk, as built earlier.

The behavior is described in the docs, but only in the known-limits page, not in the stream section where the user looked. That is a docs problem.

I reproduced the report with a mocked stream that sends two chunks and then errors. The error reaches the caller as a stream error part, and the onEvent hook reports a failure event with no attempts after the first. This matches what the user saw.

I answered with the reason and suggested two things they can do: catch the error and call the function again with the text so far as a prefix, or use a non-stream call where a retry is possible.

I moved a short version of the explanation into the stream section and linked to the known-limits page for details. I also added the mocked mid-stream test to the suite, since there was a test for failure before the first chunk but none that pins this case.

The user was fine with the answer. I labeled the issue as a question.

summary: Added a docs recipe for continuing a stream that broke in the middle, as a user-side pattern, without adding the feature to the library.
body:
Following the mid-stream question from earlier today, I wrote a recipe for people who need continuation. It collects the text received so far, and on error starts a new call with the original messages plus an assistant message holding the partial text.

I tested the recipe against a mocked model that breaks after three chunks. The second call received the right messages and the combined text had no gap. The overlap case is real: some providers repeat words when asked to continue, so the recipe says to tell the model to continue exactly where it stopped.

I considered building this into the library as an option. I decided not to. It would need to decide how to join text, deal with tool calls in the partial answer, and handle providers that do not support a prefilled assistant message. Each of those has several valid answers, so a fixed one would be wrong for someone.

The recipe is in the docs under the stream section and passes the validator. I noted on the issue that if more people ask, a hook for a continuation strategy could be considered. For now it stays user code.

summary: A user reported the bundle size grew in the last minor, and I traced it to the validation code importing a full schema helper, which I replaced with plain checks.
body:
The report said that importing the library added 11 KB more than two versions ago. I measured it with a small script that bundles an import of the library and prints the minified size.

The growth matched the options validation from earlier. The validator used a helper to describe the allowed values, and a deep import pulled in a larger part of it than needed. The size went from 6.2 KB to 17.4 KB minified.

I replaced the helper with plain checks. There are about fifteen options, each with a type and range check, so I wrote a small table of rules and one function that walks it. The error messages stay identical, and the existing validation tests are the safety net.

All the validation tests passed unchanged, which confirms that messages and behavior did not move. The bundle came down to 6.9 KB.

I added a size check to CI that fails if the bundled import goes above 8 KB, so a future dependency cannot grow it unnoticed.

summary: Released the bundle size fix as a patch together with the README example correction, and told the reporter the new numbers.
body:
The patch contains two things: the validation rewrite without the helper and the README fix that was waiting since the last release.

Before publishing I ran the full checklist: tests, type tests with the older TypeScript, the docs validator (31 examples), and the new size check. All passed.

The changeset says patch, with one line for the size and one for the README. I kept the text short so the changelog stays readable.

After the release I installed it in a clean project and measured again: 6.9 KB minified, 2.8 KB gzipped. I also checked that the README on the npm page now shows the new example for previousErrors.

I replied to the reporter with the before and after numbers and the commit that fixed it, and thanked them for the clear report with the measuring method. They answered a few minutes later that their build is smaller by the same amount.

The issue is closed. The size check is the lasting part of this work: it is a simple script in the CI workflow, and I wrote its limit in a comment next to the number.

summary: Answered a question about whether the library can respect a total time budget for all attempts, and explained how to combine it with an abort signal.
body:
A user wanted the call to give up after 20 seconds in total, including all retries and fallbacks. The library has no such option.

The existing abort handling already supports this: an abort signal stops the retries, including a wait between attempts. So the answer is to pass `AbortSignal.timeout(20000)` as the abort signal of the call.
