I verified it with a test using a mocked provider that always fails with a retryable error and a long backoff. With a 1 second timeout signal, the call ended after about one second with an abort error, and no further attempt was made.

One caveat I mentioned: an attempt that is already running is also aborted, because the signal is passed to the model. That is usually what people want for a total budget.

I added a short example to the abort docs. I did not add a budget option, since the signal covers it and a second mechanism would have to be kept consistent with it.

summary: Investigated an issue where Retry-After values given as an HTTP date were ignored, and found the parser only handled seconds; added date parsing with a cap.
body:
A user reported that a provider returned `Retry-After` as a date, and the library retried after its normal backoff and hit the limit again.

I looked at the parser from the earlier Retry-After work. It reads the header, converts it to a number and multiplies by 1000. A date string gives NaN, and the code treated NaN as no header. The spec allows both forms, so this is a real gap and I should have handled it then.

The fix parses a date when the value is not a number. The delay is the date minus the current time, and anything in the past gives zero. For tests, the clock has to be controllable, so I used Vitest fake timers and set the system time.

Then the cap question. A date far in the future, or a mistake in the provider's clock, could make the library wait for hours. Seconds had the same risk. Looking at the code, the existing maxDelay option caps the computed backoff but not the header. So a header of 3600 seconds was waited in full.

I thought about which is correct. A provider that says to wait an hour probably means it, and the caller can abort. But silently waiting an hour in a server request is bad. I decided that the header is capped by a new option `maxRetryAfter`, default 60000 ms. If the header is above the cap, the library does not wait and does not retry that model; it goes to the next fallback, or throws if there is none.

This changes behavior for people whose provider sends long values, so I want to be careful. Waiting more than a minute inside a call is rare, and I think the new default is safer. But it is a behavior change, so I will release it as a minor and write it clearly in the changeset.

Tests added:
- header as seconds, as before
- header as a date 5 seconds ahead
- header as a date in the past
- header above the cap with a fallback available
- header above the cap with no fallback
- garbage value, falling back to normal backoff

The last case surprised me: the old code and the new code both ignore garbage, but there was no test for it.

The event for a skipped model carries the reason `retry-after-too-long`, which required adding a member to the union of event types. The docs for events need that line.

Still to do: docs for the option, the events table, and a prerelease.

summary: Wrote docs for maxRetryAfter and the new skip reason, published a prerelease, and asked the reporter whether the default of one minute fits their provider.
body:
The docs page for options got an entry for `maxRetryAfter`, with the unit in milliseconds as the other entries have. I also described what happens above the cap: no wait, no retry on that model, move to the next one.

The events table got the new reason value. I checked the type test for the event union, which exhaustively switches over the reasons, and it failed to compile until I added the case. That is the intended safety net.

I wrote a short section in the Retry-After docs about the two header forms, with an example of each in the mocked provider style used elsewhere.

The validator now checks `maxRetryAfter` like the other options: it must be a non-negative number. I added tests for a negative value and for a string.

I published a prerelease. In the issue I asked the reporter two things: does their provider send long values often, and is a minute a sensible default for them.

I also asked in the comment whether anyone relies on the old behavior of waiting in full, so that people who do can speak up before the minor.

The reporter replied in the evening that their provider sends dates and values up to 30 seconds, so the default fits. I waited with the release for other comments.

summary: Released the Retry-After date support and the maxRetryAfter cap as a minor, with the behavior change spelled out at the top of the changeset.
body:
No objections came in, so I released. The changeset starts with a sentence on the behavior change: values above one minute no longer cause a wait, and users who want the old behavior can set `maxRetryAfter` to a large number.

Before the release I went through the checklist again, including the search for old shapes that I added after the README mistake. This time I searched for `Retry-After` across the repository, and found a sentence in the known-limits page that said dates are not supported. It was now wrong, so I removed it.

The workflow passed and the package was published. On a clean install I ran a small script with a mocked provider that sends a date header 2 seconds ahead; the log showed a delay of about 2000 ms.

I also tested the cap path: a header of 120 seconds with a fallback model led to a skip event with the new reason and the fallback ran immediately.

The reporter confirmed on the issue that it works with their provider. I closed the issue with the version number.

One point I want to revisit: the skipped model is not tried again later in the same call. For a call with a short list, that may be a loss, since a model skipped at the start could be available again after the others fail. It is an edge case, and nobody asked for it, so I only noted it in the planning file.

The docs validator now counts 34 examples. The size check stayed under the limit at 7.1 KB.

This finishes the Retry-After topic for now. Next I will look at the open issues again, since a few new ones came in during the week.

summary: Triaged the new issues after the Retry-After release: two questions, one docs gap and a request for a circuit breaker, which I labeled but did not start.
body:
Four issues were open since the last triage. I read each and labeled it.

The first was a question about using the library with streamObject; the answer is yes, it behaves like streamText, and I replied with the link to the stream section. The second was a question on whether fallbacks can be tried in parallel. They cannot, by design, since it would double the cost, and I said so.

The third is a docs gap: the page on per-model overrides does not say that an override of maxRetries to zero means a model is tried once. I added the sentence and a test that pins the behavior, since it was only implied by other tests.

The fourth is a request for a circuit breaker: after N failures of a model within a time window, skip it for a while. It is a larger feature, with shared state between calls, which the library does not have today. State shared across calls raises questions about memory, serverless runtimes and multiple instances.

I labeled it as a request and asked the user for their setup and why a skip within one call is not enough. I will decide on it after the answer.

The docs fix goes into the next patch.

summary: Planned a circuit breaker as an opt-in with in-memory state per wrapped model, after the requester explained a long-running server where the same model fails for minutes.
body:
The requester runs a long-lived server that makes many calls a minute. When the primary model is down, each call still tries it, retries, and only then falls back, adding several seconds to every request.

That is a case where state across calls helps, and a skip within a single call does not. So the request is reasonable. The question is how to build it without turning the library into a framework.

The design I settled on:
- An opt-in option `circuitBreaker: { failureThreshold, windowMs, cooldownMs }`.
- State lives in the closure of the wrapped model, in memory. No shared storage and no global map, so two wrapped instances do not affect each other.
- States are closed, open and half-open. After the cooldown one call is allowed through as a probe; success closes it, failure opens it again.
- When a model is open, the loop skips it with an event reason `circuit-open`, and goes to the next model.

I went through the awkward cases. Serverless functions lose the state between invocations, so the breaker does nothing there; the docs should say it is meant for long-lived processes. If all models are open, the loop should still try the last one rather than fail immediately, otherwise a short outage becomes a long one. I will choose to try the model whose cooldown ends first.

What counts as a failure matters too. Only errors classified as retryable should count, so that a bad prompt with a 400 error does not open the breaker. That ties it to the classifier, including the context version added recently.

Abort errors must not count either, since the caller cancelled them.

The time source has to be replaceable in tests. I will reuse the internal clock approach from the Retry-After work and use fake timers.

I considered a per-call-window design, where the window slides over the last N calls instead of time, and rejected it. Time windows are easier to explain and to test.

Order of work: type tests, the state machine as a pure module with its own tests, then the wiring in the shared loop, then events and docs. The pure module can be tested without any model mocks.

I wrote the plan into the issue and asked the requester to check the three states and the defaults. I suggested a threshold of 5, a window of 30 seconds and a cooldown of 30 seconds as starting values, but they will not be defaults: the option has to be set with all three values.

summary: Wrote the circuit breaker state machine as a pure module with fake-timer tests covering closed, open, half-open and the window expiry.
body:
The module is `src/breaker.ts`, with no imports from the rest of the library. It exposes `createBreaker(options, now)` and the methods `canAttempt()`, `recordSuccess()` and `recordFailure()`.

Failures are stored as timestamps and the ones older than the window are dropped when read. When the count reaches the threshold, the state becomes open and records the time. After the cooldown, `canAttempt` returns true once and sets half-open, so only one probe goes through.

The tests cover:
- opening exactly at the threshold, not before
- failures outside the window not counting
- a probe success closing it and clearing failures
- a probe failure opening it again with a fresh cooldown
- a second caller during half-open being refused

All nine tests pass with a fake clock passed in as the `now` function, so no real timers are involved.

summary: Wired the circuit breaker into the shared loop, counting only retryable errors, and handled the all-models-open case by trying the one whose cooldown ends first.
body:
In the loop, each model now has an optional breaker created once when the library is applied to the model list, so the state lives as long as the wrapped model.

Before an attempt, the loop asks the breaker. If it is open, the loop emits a skip event with the reason `circuit-open` and moves on. After a failure, the loop records it only if the classifier said the error is retryable and it is not an abort. A success records a success.

The all-open case needed a decision in code. If every model refuses, the loop picks the one with the earliest cooldown end and forces an attempt. For that I added a `forceProbe()` method that returns the time until the cooldown ends and lets the loop choose.

Tests: a primary that fails five times opens the breaker and the sixth call goes straight to the fallback with one skip event; a 400 error never counts; an abort never counts; all models open still produces an attempt instead of an immediate error.

The existing suite passed unchanged, since the option is off by default. Left to do: the type tests I should have written first, which I wrote after this time, plus the docs and a prerelease.

summary: Wrote the circuit breaker docs with a long-lived server example and a clear note about serverless, then published a prerelease and asked the requester to run it under real load.
body:
The docs section opens with who needs this: processes that live long and make many calls, where one model is down for minutes. The second paragraph says in plain words that serverless functions lose the state between invocations, so the breaker will not help there.

I described the three states with a small diagram in text form, and each of the three options with its unit. All three are required when the option is set, and validation throws a clear error if one is missing, which I wrote tests for.

The example uses the values suggested in the plan: a threshold of 5, a window and a cooldown of 30000 ms each. It went through the docs validator test, which now checks 37 examples.

The events table got the `circuit-open` reason, and the exhaustive type test forced me to handle it everywhere, as it did the last time.

While writing, I noticed that two wrapped models created from the same config do not share state, which is by design but easy to miss. I added a warning sentence, and a test that two instances are independent.

I also wrote the type tests that were still missing from the implementation step. They check that the option rejects a missing field and accepts the full object, and they pass.

The size check went to 7.9 KB, close to the 8 KB limit. I looked at what grew: the breaker module is small, and most of the growth is the loop wiring. I raised the limit to 9 KB with a comment on why, since the feature is real, but I want to keep an eye on it.

The changeset is a minor with one line. I published a prerelease and installed it into a scratch server project, where I ran a mocked provider that fails for 40 seconds. The log showed the skip events beginning after the fifth failure, and the first probe after 30 seconds.

I asked the requester to try it under real load and to report the skip events they see. I will release after their answer.

summary: The circuit breaker prerelease held up under the requester's load test, but one run showed the half-open probe letting several calls through at once, so I limited it to a single probe.
body:
The requester ran the prerelease against their long-running server overnight and posted the logs this morning. The breaker opened correctly after five retryable failures in the window and stayed open for the cooldown. The problem was in the half-open state: when cooldown ended, about a dozen concurrent requests all saw half-open and all went to the failing model.

The state machine was pure and each call asked it for the current state, so nothing marked a probe as taken. I added a probeInFlight flag to the state in src/circuit-breaker.ts. The first caller that sees half-open takes the probe, and the others are treated as open until the probe settles.

A failed probe sends the breaker back to open with a fresh cooldown. A successful one closes it and clears the failure window. I also made sure a probe that is aborted by the caller's signal releases the flag without counting as a failure. Without that, an abort would have left the breaker stuck in half-open forever.

I wrote three fake-timer tests: ten parallel calls at the end of the cooldown produce exactly one probe, a failed probe reopens, and an aborted probe frees the slot. The existing breaker tests passed unchanged. I reproduced the original bug first with a test that counted calls to the mocked model, and it saw 10 calls before the fix and 1 after.

I have not published yet. Next I want to publish a second prerelease and ask the requester to rerun the same overnight test, and look at whether the all-models-open path needs the same probe rule.

summary: The second circuit breaker prerelease ran a full night on the requester's server with no extra calls to the failing model, and I applied one small change to the log event names before the release.
body:
The requester reported back this morning. Under the same load as before, the failing model received exactly one probe per cooldown, and the fallback model handled the rest. They counted 41 breaker openings over the night, each followed by a single probe.

They asked about the log events. The hook currently emits 'circuit-open' and 'circuit-half-open' but nothing when the breaker closes again, so their dashboard could not show recovery time. I added a 'circuit-close' event with the model index and how long the breaker had been open.

I also renamed the event field from model to modelIndex in the breaker events so it matches the other logging events. The prerelease had not been promoted, so this is not a breaking change for anyone on a stable version. I updated the type tests and the docs table of events.

The all-models-open case now uses the same single-probe rule, which I checked with a test where both models are open and ten calls arrive after one cooldown ends. I left the changeset as a minor, with a note that the breaker is opt-in and off by default. The release goes out after the requester confirms the new event.

summary: Released the circuit breaker as a minor and then fixed a bug found within hours: the failure window counted errors from before the breaker was enabled on a hot-reloaded config.
body:
The minor went out this afternoon with the breaker, the close event and the docs. I closed the feature issue and posted the changelog link for the requester.

This evening a new user opened an issue. They use a dev server with hot reload, and each reload creates the wrapped model again. The breaker state is kept per wrapped model in memory, so every reload should have started with a clean state. Instead they saw the breaker open on the first call after a reload.

I reproduced it with a small script that created two wrapped models in a row with the same model object. The state lived in a WeakMap keyed by the underlying model, not the wrapper. That key was my choice, made so that the same model wrapped in two places would share one breaker. It worked as designed for that case, but it means a reload that keeps the same provider object keeps the old failure window.

I considered three fixes. One was to key by the wrapper, which loses the sharing. Another was to add a breaker key option that defaults to the model object. The third was to expire the window by time only, which already happens. I chose the key option, because sharing a breaker across places is something the requester wants for their server, and a reload user can pass a fresh key.

I added the option as circuitBreaker.key, typed as an object or string, and wrote tests for the shared default and for two separate keys. The docs got a short section on dev servers. I did not publish yet. I asked the reporter whether a documented key is enough for them, since an automatic reset on reload cannot be detected from inside a library.

summary: Went through the issue list after the circuit breaker fix and sorted what is real: two type reports, a logging question and a docs gap, so the next work is the options typing.
body:
I spent the evening on the issue list after the breaker patch went out. There were eleven open issues and I read each one again with the current code in mind. Four turned out to be answered by existing options, and I replied with short examples and closed two of them.

Three reports described the same symptom: passing a backoff object with a shorthand number in the same position did not narrow, and the editor showed an error that pointed at the wrong line. One of them used exactOptionalPropertyTypes and got a different error for the same shape. I reproduced all three in a scratch file with the current published types, so they are real and not a user setup problem.

The logging question asked whether the hook receives the model id. It does, but the docs never say so, so I wrote it down as a docs gap with a label. I also left the request for a per-call budget open for now, since it needs a decision first. Tomorrow I will write the type tests that fail today, before touching any of the unions, and then decide how to split the types.

summary: Triaged the issue list and chose to work on the typing of the options object first, because three separate reports came down to the same unions that do not narrow.
body:
After the breaker releases I went through all open issues. There are seven. Two are questions that I answered with links to docs. One is a feature request for a per-call attempt budget that I labeled for later. Three are about the types of the options, and one is about the docs.

The three type reports have the same root. The options type is a union of a plain object and a function returning options, and a few fields are unions of a number and an object. Users hit errors like "Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'BackoffOptions'" when they spread a shared base config into a per-model override. One user also reported that hovering over the options in their editor shows a huge expanded type that cannot be read.

I wrote a small file of the failing usages from the three issues as type tests, using expectTypeOf, and confirmed all three fail today. Then I traced the causes in src/types.ts. The override type was built with a Partial of the full options, which pulls in the nested object fields as partial as well and mixes them with the number shorthand.

My plan has three steps. First, split the number shorthand and the object form of backoff into two named types so errors point at the right one. Second, make the override type explicit instead of derived with Partial. Third, export the named types so users can write their shared base config with a real type name.

I will do this in order and check the type tests after each step. The per-call attempt budget stays on the list. I replied on each of the three issues to say the fix is planned and what the plan is, and asked one reporter for their tsconfig since they use exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which may behave differently.

summary: Split the backoff option into named shorthand and object types and made the override type explicit; two of the three type issues now pass as type tests.
body:
I started with the named types. In src/types.ts, BackoffOptions is now the object form only, and a separate BackoffInput is the union of a number and BackoffOptions. The number shorthand still means a base delay in milliseconds, so behavior does not change.

The error messages are better. Before, assigning a string gave a long message listing every member of a nested union. Now it names BackoffInput, and the editor hover shows the alias instead of an expanded literal.

Next I replaced the derived override type. It was Partial of the full options minus a few keys, and it made nested objects partial. The new ModelOverride is written out field by field. It has seven fields, each optional, and backoff uses BackoffInput. I checked each field against the docs table so none were lost.

The type tests from the issues: the spread of a shared base config into an override passes now. The hover size complaint is not testable, but I measured the declaration output instead. The emitted d.ts for the options went from 212 lines to 148.

The third issue, with exactOptionalPropertyTypes, still fails. The reporter sent the tsconfig. With that flag on, passing an explicit undefined for an optional field is an error, and their wrapper code builds options with undefined values for unset fields. That is the flag working as intended, but the library types could accept undefined for each optional field without harm.

I decided to allow it, since a user building options conditionally is common, and the runtime already treats undefined as unset. I have not changed that yet. It touches every optional field, and I want to do it with a test that checks each key. That is for the next session.

summary: Allowed explicit undefined on every optional option field, with a test that walks all keys, which fixed the exactOptionalPropertyTypes report.
body:
I changed each optional field in the options and override types to accept undefined explicitly. Eleven fields in total, counting the ones nested under backoff and the breaker.

To be sure nothing was missed, I wrote a type test that builds an object with every key set to undefined and checks that it is assignable under a tsconfig with exactOptionalPropertyTypes on. Vitest typecheck uses a separate tsconfig for this, so I added one to the test folder.

The first run found two missed fields, both in the breaker options. After fixing them the test passed. I also checked the runtime: the defaults merge uses an explicit undefined check, so undefined falls back to the default value. A small runtime test covers it. I will export the named types next and then release.

summary: Exported the named option types, wrote a docs section on typing a shared base config, and released the type fixes as a patch.
body:
With the types fixed, the last step was to let users name them. I exported BackoffOptions, BackoffInput, ModelOverride, CircuitBreakerOptions and the context type for classify from the package entry. Some were exported already, so I checked the generated index.d.ts to see the final list instead of trusting the source.

I then added a test that imports every public type name from the built package, not from src. It reads the tsdown output, so a type that is exported in source but dropped from the bundle would be caught. It passed.

The docs got a new section called typing a shared config. The example defines a const base with the type ModelOverride, spreads it into two overrides, and changes only the backoff. I ran the example through tsc to confirm it compiles, using the exact snippet from the markdown file. I do this for docs examples now, after the README mistake from a few weeks ago.

The changeset is a patch, because nothing changes at runtime and the types only accept more than before. I wrote that sentence in the changeset, with the one exception: error messages for wrong values will read differently, so someone matching on text of a compiler error would see a change. That seemed too unlikely to need a minor.

The release workflow ran green and the package went out. I commented on all three issues with the version number. Two reporters confirmed within the hour that their code compiles. The third, with the strict flag, said the conditional build of options now works without a cast, and they deleted their cast.

What is left from this topic: the per-call attempt budget request, which is a feature and not a type problem, and a README pointer to the new typing section.

summary: Added the README pointer to the typing section and a short section for the breaker, and cut the README by moving the long examples into the docs.
body:
The README had grown with each release, and after the breaker it was about 340 lines. Users who open the package page see all of it, so I trimmed it tonight.

I kept the install, the basic retry example, the fallback example, and one short table of options. The long sections on streams, Retry-After, jitter comparison, classify context and the breaker now have two lines each and a link to the matching docs page. Before moving anything I checked that each moved section already exists in the docs, and two did not fully: the stream notes had a paragraph that was only in the README. I moved it first.

I added a line in the options table pointing to the typing section, with the exported type names. The breaker gets a three-line example with a note that it is opt-in and in memory only.

I ran the README snippets through tsc, as with the docs. One of them still used the removed old name of an option from two minors back. It compiled only because of a loose any in my check script. I fixed both the snippet and the check script, so now it uses the real package types.

The README is now about 120 lines. Links use the stable docs URL, so they will not break when versions change. I added a changeset marked as docs only with no version bump, so the page on npm updates with the next release. Nothing else changed in the library today.

summary: Looked into the per-call attempt budget request and decided against a new option, because maxAttempts passed per call through providerOptions would be more surprising than helpful.
body:
The request is to set a different number of attempts for a single call, for example one call in a user flow that must fail fast while the rest of the app uses the default. The requester suggested a new field on the call options.

I first checked what the AI SDK gives a middleware at call time. The call parameters include providerOptions, which is the place users would put it. Putting library settings there means they travel with the call to the provider, and some providers reject unknown keys. I tested this with the mock provider that validates keys, and it failed with an unknown option error, so the library would have to strip its own key. That is doable but fragile.

The other way is to create a second wrapped model for the fail-fast path. The wrapping is cheap and holds no connection. I measured creating a wrapped model, and it took under a millisecond. The only cost is the breaker, which is shared by key anyway. If the user passes the same key to both, they share the breaker state, which is probably what they want.

So my answer was to use a second wrapped model with maxAttempts set to one, sharing the breaker key. I wrote the example and tested that it runs: two wrappers over one model, one with a single attempt, and both feeding the same breaker. The test checks that failures from the fail-fast wrapper count toward the shared window.

I added this as a recipe in the docs. I replied to the requester with the reasons and the recipe. I said I would reconsider if many people ask, since it would be a feature with a real cost in the API. I left the issue open with a label for a week to give them time to answer.

summary: The attempt budget requester accepted the two-wrapper recipe and closed the issue, so nothing was added to the library.
body:
The requester wrote back this morning. They tried the recipe in their app with a fail-fast wrapper for the checkout flow and a normal one for the chat. It worked, and the shared breaker key made the fail-fast path skip a model that the chat path had already found to be down.

They asked for one thing: a line in the docs saying that the two wrappers share breaker state only if they use the same key. The recipe already used the key in the code but did not say it in words. I added the sentence.

I closed the issue. The open issue count is now three: a docs gap on stream errors, a question about logging in edge runtimes, and a request I had not read closely yet.

summary: Checked the logging hooks in an edge runtime and found that the default logger used console methods that are missing in one runtime, so I made the hook calls safe when console is partial.
body:
The question from the issue list was whether the logging hooks work on an edge runtime. I assumed yes, since the library has no Node imports, and verified it by bundling a test entry for a worker-like environment and running it in a Vitest environment that mimics one.

The retry logic itself ran fine. The failure was in the optional default logger, which calls console.debug and console.warn. In the reporter's runtime, console.debug is not a function, and the hook threw a TypeError inside the retry loop. The error then looked like a model failure, and it was counted as an attempt. That second part was the real bug: an exception from a logging hook must never change the result of the call.

I fixed it in two places. The default logger checks that each console method exists and falls back to console.log. And the loop now calls every hook inside a try and catch, so a user hook that throws is swallowed and reported once with the warning channel. I did not want a silent swallow, so the warning is shown one time per wrapped model.

Tests: a hook that throws on the first call, and the call still succeeds on the second attempt with the attempt count of 2, not 3. Another test sets console.debug to undefined and checks that the default logger does not throw.

I documented that hooks are not allowed to affect the outcome, and that errors in hooks are swallowed after one warning. That is a behavior change in the strict sense, because before a throwing hook failed the call. I judged it a bug fix, and I put it at the top of the patch changeset so no one is surprised.

The patch will go out with the next batch of small fixes. The reporter has a build to try.

summary: Wrote the docs fix for stream errors and found while testing the examples that a stream failing before the first chunk with an abort signal already set threw the wrong error type.
body:
The open docs gap said it is not clear which errors the stream retry covers. I rewrote the stream page with a table: error before the first chunk is retried, error after the first chunk is passed to the caller, abort at any point stops everything. Each row has a short code example.

As I always do now, I ran every example as a test. The abort row failed. When the signal was already aborted before the call started, the stream function threw the last error from the model instead of an AbortError. In the non-stream path the same case was right, so the two paths differed.

The cause was in the stream wrapper's start function. It checked the signal only after the first attempt, in the catch block, and then threw the stored error. The non-stream path checks before the first attempt. I moved the check to the top of the attempt loop in the shared code, so both paths use it. That also removes the duplicate check I found in the stream file.

I added three tests for an already aborted signal: generate, stream before the first chunk and stream after the first chunk. All three expect an AbortError, and the mock model records zero calls in the first two cases. Before the fix the stream case recorded one call.

I also verified the reason property. The AI SDK passes through signal.reason, and a custom reason is kept as the error cause. The test uses a custom reason object and checks it.

Then I finished the table in the docs, with the corrected behavior. The throwing-hook fix from the other day and this fix will go out together as a patch. I wrote the changeset with two bullet points. The abort fix is a bug, and the edge runtime one is a bug too, so a patch is the right bump.

I released it in the afternoon after the CI run.

summary: Found that a stream failing before the first chunk with an abort signal already set threw the wrong error type, and fixed it so the abort error comes first, with tests.
body:
While checking the stream examples for the docs fix, one case behaved oddly. A stream call that failed before the first chunk, with the abort signal already aborted, threw the provider error instead of the abort error. The plain non-stream path did the right thing, so the two paths had drifted apart.

I wrote a failing test first. It builds a mocked model whose stream rejects at once, passes an already aborted signal, and expects the error to be the signal's reason. The test failed with the mocked provider error, as the user would have seen it.

The cause was in the stream branch of the shared loop. It caught the error, ran the classify step, and only then looked at the signal before sleeping. With a signal that was aborted before the first attempt, the loop never reached that check, because a non-retryable error was rethrown straight away. The non-stream path checks the signal at the top of each iteration, which is why it was fine.

I moved the signal check into one small helper and called it at the top of every attempt in both paths, and again right after a failure is caught. If the signal is aborted at that moment, the abort reason is thrown and the provider error is dropped. I kept the earlier rule that an abort during a sleep also throws the abort reason.

I added three more tests: aborted before the call, aborted during the first attempt, and aborted during a backoff sleep, each for both generate and stream. All of them pass now, and the whole suite is green. The logging hook does not fire for an attempt that never started, and I added an assertion for that as well.

The docs example that showed this case now matches the real behavior, so I left its text alone. I added a patch changeset that describes the change as a fix to the error type. Next I will finish the stream docs fix and release both together.

summary: Released the once-per-isolate warning fix as a patch and the edge runtime reporter confirmed a single warning per worker.
body:
I read the diff again this morning and found nothing to change. The module-level set is small, keyed by warning name and hook name, and the reset function is only reachable from the internal test path.

The patch went out after CI. The reporter tested it in their worker and saw one warning in the log across about two hundred requests, which matches the isolate lifetime they expected.

They asked whether the library could keep breaker state across requests in a worker. I explained that in-memory state cannot do this, and that a shared store would be a different feature with an interface for storage, which I do not plan now. I added their use case to the circuit breaker issue as a comment, in case it comes up again.

summary: Started planning the breaking release, listing which deprecated options to remove and writing the migration notes first so that the list stays small and justified.
body:
There are four things in the code that I marked as deprecated over the last months and that I would like to remove in the next major version. I wrote them down with the reason and the replacement for each.

First, the old maxRetries name, which was kept as an alias of maxAttempts. The two differ by one in meaning, and that has caused confusion in three issues. Second, the onRetry hook that takes positional arguments, replaced by the event-based hooks. Third, the string form of the fallback list, where a model id was accepted and resolved through the AI SDK global provider. Fourth, the default of full jitter being applied when the user passes a backoff number, which should stay, so I took it off the list.

So the list has three items. I searched the issues and the discussion for each one to see how much it is used. I cannot see downloads per option, so I used the issues, and I also searched public code on GitHub for the option names. maxRetries appears in many places, mostly copied from the README of an early version. onRetry is rarer. The string fallback is almost unused.

Because maxRetries is common, I do not want to just delete it. My plan is to keep it in the major version but make it throw a clear error with the migration message, for one major, and only then remove it. The error text names maxAttempts and states the off-by-one difference. For onRetry the same: a clear error that points to the hooks.

I started the migration guide before writing any code, because the guide shows whether the changes are explainable in a few lines each. Each of the three items got a before and an after snippet, and a codemod-free instruction, since a find and replace is enough for the first two.

I also checked the peer dependency range. The library supports one major of the AI SDK and one older, and I would like to drop the older one in the same release, since it halves the test matrix. I will check how the older one is used by looking at the install stats on the issue tracker, which is thin evidence. I will ask in a pinned issue before I decide.

I opened a pinned discussion titled with the planned removals, listing the three items and asking for objections, with a two week window. No code changes were made today.

summary: Two people answered the pinned discussion: one needs the older AI SDK major supported a while longer, so I will keep it and drop only the three deprecated options.
body:
Over the last few days the discussion got two answers. The first said that removing the throwing error for maxRetries is fine and asked only for a clear message. The second works in a company codebase that is stuck on the older AI SDK major for a few more months, and asked me not to drop that range in this release.

That is a fair request and it costs me little. The test matrix already runs both majors in CI and it has been stable. Dropping it would save only some minutes of CI time. I decided to keep the older range in this major and to announce its removal for the next one, with a date-free statement in the docs: it is supported until the next major of this library.

I wrote this in the discussion. I also asked the second person which minor of the older AI SDK they use, because I want to make sure the CI matrix includes it, and they answered that it is the last minor of that line, which the matrix does cover.

The scope of the breaking release is now: three removals that throw clear errors, no change in peer dependencies. I updated the migration guide draft to say this and removed the section about the SDK range. Implementation starts next.

summary: Implemented the clear errors for maxRetries, the positional onRetry and the string fallback, each with the migration message and a test that checks the message text.
body:
I made the three changes in order, with the tests first.

For maxRetries: the options validation now sees the key and throws a ConfigError. The message reads: "maxRetries was removed in v2. Use maxAttempts, which counts the first call, so maxRetries: 2 becomes maxAttempts: 3." I used the same ConfigError class that the validation already throws for bad values, so users can catch one type. The test checks the full message, since the message is the migration help.

For onRetry: the old hook took the error, the attempt and the delay as positional arguments. If a user passes onRetry, validation throws with a pointer to the onAttemptFailed event hook and a one line example. I did not try to translate the old hook into the new one, because that would keep two APIs alive.

For the string fallback, the list items are now checked at wrap time. If an item is a string, the error says to pass a model object, and shows resolving it with the provider the user already has. The old code resolved it through the global provider, and I removed that code, along with the import it needed. That trimmed the bundle by a small amount, about 0.4 kB after minification.

I had to be careful that the errors come at wrap time, not at the first failing call. A configuration error that appears only during an outage would be the worst kind. I added a test that wraps with each removed option and expects the throw before any model is called, using a mock that fails the test if it is called.

Types: I removed the three from the public types, so TypeScript users get a compile error first. The runtime errors are for JavaScript users and for anyone using a cast. I added type tests that expect errors on each removed key, with ts-expect-error.

The docs and the README were searched for the old names. Three places still mentioned maxRetries, all in the explanation of defaults, and I fixed them. The changeset is a major with the migration text. I left the publishing for after the prerelease.

summary: Published a prerelease of the major and asked the discussion participants to try the upgrade, with the migration guide linked in the changeset and the pinned discussion.
body:
I finished the migration guide this morning. It has one section per removed item, each with a before and an after snippet, and a short checklist at the top: search for maxRetries, onRetry, and string items in the fallback list.

All the snippets in the guide were compiled by the docs snippet test, with both the old and the new versions. The old snippets are expected to fail with the specific error, so the test checks that the failure is the message I wrote. This keeps the guide and the real messages in sync.

The prerelease was published under the next tag. I checked by installing it in a clean folder with the older AI SDK major and then the newer one, and ran a small script that wraps a mock model with each. Both worked, and each removed option threw the expected message.

I posted in the pinned discussion with the install command and asked the two people who answered to try it on their code. I also asked the person on the older AI SDK major to run their own tests against it, since that is the combination I care most about.

The plan is to wait about a week for feedback and release the major if nothing serious shows up. In the meantime I will not merge new features, so the release stays small. Open issues are two docs questions that I can answer without code changes.

summary: The user on the older AI SDK major found that the prerelease compiled but their own types broke, because the exported option types referenced a type that exists only in the newer SDK.
body:
The feedback came in this morning. Their code ran fine, but the build failed with an error about a missing export from the AI SDK in the library's declaration file: a type named in one of the middleware option types does not exist in their older version.

I reproduced it by installing the older major in a scratch project and running tsc with skipLibCheck set to false, which is what they have on. My own CI used skipLibCheck, so it never saw this. That is a gap in the CI setup and not only in the code.

The type came in with the breaking release because I changed the context type for classify to reuse a call-options type from the newer SDK instead of writing the few fields out. It was a small shortcut of mine in this release, so the problem is only in the prerelease and no stable version has it.

The fix was to define the call-options shape locally with only the fields the library reads, and make it structurally compatible with both SDK majors. I checked that by assigning the real type from each version to the local one in a type test, run once per SDK major in the matrix.

The CI change: the type test job now runs with skipLibCheck false for the matrix entry of the older SDK, and it fails if the declaration file refers to anything missing. I confirmed the job turns red on the previous commit by running it against the prerelease tag.

I published a second prerelease and asked the user to install it. They confirmed the build passes with their strict settings, about an hour later. I also asked the other participant to rerun their check. The release is still planned for a few days from now, and I will add the changed CI step to the notes for the maintainers of the repo, which is only me.

summary: Released the major version after the second prerelease got no further reports, and spent the evening answering the first upgrade questions, one of which exposed an unclear sentence in the guide.
body:
Both participants confirmed the second prerelease, and a week passed without new reports, so I released the major this afternoon. The changeset text starts with the three removals and links to the migration guide. I checked the release notes on GitHub after the workflow ran, and the formatting was right.

I also moved the latest tag and checked npm view for the dist-tags, since a prerelease tag left behind caused confusion once before. The next tag now points to the same version, which I accept for the day.

Three questions arrived in the evening. The first user upgraded and got the maxRetries error. They said the message was clear, and they fixed it in a minute. That is the outcome I hoped for from the design.

The second user was confused about the off-by-one. They had maxRetries: 3 and changed it to maxAttempts: 3, which makes one less call than before. The guide said maxAttempts counts the first call, but only in a footnote. The error message states it, but they had read the guide first. I moved the sentence to the first line of that section and added a small table with maxRetries values 0 to 3 and the matching maxAttempts values, which shows the difference at a glance.

The third question was about onRetry. The user wanted the same positional arguments in the new hook. I explained that the event object holds the same three values under the names error, attempt and delayMs, and I added a before and after for exactly that case in the guide. The mapping was in the docs for the hooks but not in the migration section, which is where people look.

Both guide changes are docs only, so they go out with the next release. I committed them and checked the snippet test again, and it passed with the table. No bugs were reported yet. I will watch the issues for the next days, and the next step on the list is the deprecation notice for the older SDK range.

summary: Added a deprecation notice for the older AI SDK range to the docs and to a runtime-free note in the README, without any code change.
body:
With the major out, I wrote down the plan for the older AI SDK range. It stays supported until the next major of this library, and I do not know when that will be. The notice says exactly that, without a date.

I put it in three places: the compatibility table in the docs, a line in the README under installation, and the migration guide as a note for people who stay on the older range. A runtime warning seemed wrong, because it would spam logs for people who cannot change their version.

I checked that the compatibility table still matches the CI matrix: both majors, the last minor of each. It does. The docs-only changeset has no version bump.

summary: Triaged the first week of issues after the major: no regressions, one question about the ConfigError class being catchable, which led to exporting it from the package entry.
body:
Since the release there are four new issues. Two are upgrade questions that the guide already answers, and I replied with the links. One is a feature request for a callback when the breaker closes, which exists as the circuit-close event, so I pointed to the docs section on events.

The fourth asked how to catch the new configuration errors. The user wrote a try and catch around the wrapping and wanted to check for the class, but ConfigError was not exported from the entry, so the instanceof check was not possible. They compared the message text instead, which is fragile.

This was my oversight. The class existed since the first version but was only used internally, and the new errors made it matter. I exported ConfigError from the entry and added it to the public types test, which reads the built package. I also added a code property with a stable string for each case, such as removed-option, so users can branch without matching text.

It is a minor addition and goes into the next release with a changeset.

summary: Triaged the second week of issues after the major release: one real bug in fallback ordering with a custom retryable check, and two usage questions answered with docs links.
body:
The second week after the major brought three new issues. Two were questions: one about combining a circuit breaker with a fallback list, and one about whether the library retries errors thrown by tools. I answered both and linked the matching docs sections. The tools one turned out to be a misunderstanding, since the library only wraps the model call and never sees tool execution errors.

The third issue was real. A user passed a custom retryable function that returned false for a 400 response, and the library still moved on to the next model in the fallback list. I reproduced it with a mocked provider in a Vitest case that throws an APICallError with statusCode 400 and isRetryable set to false.

The cause was in the shared loop. The check for retryable errors ran before the custom function, and the fallback path was entered whenever the retry attempts for the current model were exhausted, even when the loop had stopped on the first attempt because of a non retryable verdict. So the verdict ended the retries for the model but not the walk through the list.

I wrote the failing test first and confirmed it fails with the message 'expected 1 call, got 2'. I did not fix it yet, because I want to look at how the fallback decision is shared between generate and stream before changing the loop. I labeled the issue as a bug and told the reporter that the cause is found and a patch is next. The two question issues were closed after the reporters confirmed the answers.

summary: Fixed the fallback running after a non retryable verdict by returning a stop reason from the attempt step, so the loop only moves to the next model when the error was retryable.
body:
This was the fix for the issue from last week, where a custom retryable function returning false still let the loop move on to the next model. The failing test from that session was waiting in the repo.

The attempt step used to return only success or the last error. I changed it to return a small result with a reason: succeeded, exhausted or stopped. The loop now treats stopped as final and throws the error right away, while exhausted still moves to the next model in the list.

Both the generate path and the stream path use the same step, so one change covered both. I added a stream test too, where the failure comes before the first chunk and the custom function says no. It passed after the change.

One thing I checked was the circuit breaker. A stopped verdict should not count as a breaker failure, since the error was judged not worth retrying and says nothing about the health of the model. The breaker already counts only retryable errors, so no change was needed there, and I added a test to keep it that way.

I also read the changelog for the earlier fallback work to make sure nobody depends on the old behavior. The README never promised that a non retryable error falls back, and the docs say the opposite in one place. I wrote a changeset as a patch and published it. The reporter replied within an hour that their case works now.

summary: Answered a question about why onRetry fires once for a stream that fails before the first chunk, and found the docs never said what counts as an attempt for streams.
body:
A user asked why their onRetry hook fired only once while their dashboard showed the model failing three times. I asked for a log and saw that two of the failures happened after the first chunk had already been sent to the client.

That is by design. The library only retries a stream that fails before the first chunk, because after that the consumer has already received data and a second attempt would repeat text. Failures after the first chunk are passed on as errors, and the hook does not fire for them.

The design is right, but the docs only mentioned it in a single sentence under the stream section. I rewrote that part with a short timeline of a stream: before the first chunk, retried; after it, passed on. I added an example of reading the error from the stream's onError callback in the AI SDK.

I replied to the user with the explanation and the link. They asked whether an option could retry mid-stream, and I said no, with the reason that there is no safe way to merge two partial outputs. I did not open a feature issue for it. The docs change went out with the next release, and nothing in the code changed.

summary: Reviewed a pull request from a user that adds a jitter option for the delay cap, and asked for a test and a smaller diff before merging.
body:
A contributor opened the first pull request to the library in a while. It adds an option to cap the jittered delay at a maximum, so that a long exponential backoff does not exceed a limit set by the user.

The idea is good, and the existing maxDelay option already does most of it, so I first checked whether the request was already covered. It was not quite: maxDelay caps the base delay before jitter is applied, so the final delay could go above it by the jitter amount.

The pull request fixed that by clamping after jitter, but it also renamed two internal helpers and reformatted a file, which made the diff hard to read. I asked them to remove the renames and to add a test with a seeded random source that proves the delay never exceeds the cap.

I also asked for a docs line saying that the cap now applies after jitter. I did not want to introduce a second option, so I suggested changing the meaning of maxDelay only if the existing tests still pass, and called it a fix rather than a feature. The contributor agreed and said they would push an update.

summary: Merged the jitter cap pull request after the contributor added a test and cut the diff, and noted a follow-up for the docs wording of the new option.
body:
The contributor came back this morning with the revised pull request for the jitter option on the delay cap. The first version touched the backoff module, the option types and an unrelated formatting pass over three files. I had asked for a test and a smaller diff, and the new one dropped the formatting changes and kept only the cap logic and the type addition.

I read the change again line by line. The jitter is now applied before the cap, so a delay can never exceed maxDelay, which is the behavior the contributor wanted and the one I had hoped for. The earlier version applied it after the cap and could produce a delay of up to 1.5 times the cap.

The new test uses a seeded random function and checks that fifty consecutive delays with a cap of 2000 ms all stay at or below 2000. It also covers the case where jitter is switched off, so the old exact delays are unchanged. I ran the full suite locally and it passed, and CI was green on the pull request.

I pulled the branch and tried one edge case by hand: a cap smaller than the base delay. The result was the cap itself, with jitter only reducing it, which seems right. I added a second small test for that case directly on the branch with the contributor's permission.

The option name was the one remaining point. The contributor called it jitterCap, which reads oddly, because the option is about whether jitter respects the cap. I kept the name to avoid another round, since renaming costs them more time than it saves readers. I will explain it better in the docs instead.

I merged with a squash and added a changeset marked as a minor. Next I will write the docs paragraph with a short example, and then release it together with whatever else is waiting. I thanked the contributor in the pull request and mentioned that the tests were what made merging easy.

summary: Investigated a report that timeouts from the provider were not retried, and found that the error arrived as a plain TypeError from fetch instead of an APICallError.
body:
A user reported that when their provider's network connection dropped, the library threw right away with no retry. They were on the latest version and had default options.

I asked for the error and got this: 'TypeError: fetch failed', with a cause of ECONNRESET. The retryable check in the library accepted APICallError with isRetryable set, and it recognized the abort and timeout errors from the AI SDK. A bare TypeError from fetch matched none of these.

I looked at how the AI SDK handles this. Most provider packages wrap the failure in an APICallError, but some paths do not, in particular when a custom fetch is passed in. So the library saw a raw error.

I considered treating every TypeError as retryable and decided against it, since a TypeError can also be a plain bug in user code, and retrying a bug three times only delays the report. Instead I want to look at the cause. A TypeError whose message is 'fetch failed' and whose cause has a code like ECONNRESET, ETIMEDOUT, ECONNREFUSED or EAI_AGAIN is a network failure.

I wrote tests with four such causes that fail now, plus a test with a plain TypeError that must stay non retryable. I wrote the helper that reads the cause code but did not wire it in yet. The user offered to test a prerelease, so I will publish one after the wiring. I also need to check how the cause looks in other runtimes, since the shape of the error differs between Node and the edge runtime.

summary: Wired the network error detection into the retryable check, handled the different error shapes across runtimes, and published a prerelease for the reporter.
body:
I finished the work from two days ago on network errors that arrive as a raw TypeError. The helper reads the cause code and the wiring into the retryable check was short.

The harder part was the runtimes. In Node, undici puts the code on error.cause.code. In the edge runtime I tested last time, the message is different, 'Network connection lost', and there is no cause at all. So code only checking the cause would miss it.

I added a small list of message patterns for the two edge runtime messages I could confirm, and kept the list short and commented with where each message was seen. I did not add patterns I could not verify, because guessing messages makes the check hard to trust.

The tests cover Node style errors with four codes, the two edge messages, and the plain TypeError that stays non retryable. I also added a test that an error with a cause that is itself an APICallError is handled as before.

The circuit breaker counts these as retryable failures now, which is right, since a connection that keeps dropping is exactly what it should react to. I checked this with one test.

I wrote a changeset as a minor, because the set of retried errors grows, and spelled that out at the top as I did for the Retry-After release. Then I published a prerelease and wrote to the reporter with the install command. Next I want to look at whether the docs list of retried errors needs an update, and it does, so that is the next small task.

summary: The reporter confirmed that the prerelease retries their dropped connections, so I updated the docs list of retried errors and released the network error support as a minor.
body:
The reporter ran the prerelease against their provider and wrote back that a forced connection reset now leads to a second attempt and a normal answer. They also sent a log with the onRetry hook, which shows the error and the delay as expected.

I updated the docs page that lists which errors are retried. It now has a separate row for network failures, with the Node codes and a note about the edge runtime messages, and a sentence saying that a plain TypeError is not retried.

I also added a line on how to extend the check for a runtime that is not covered, by passing a retryable function in the options. An example in the docs shows a function that adds one more message pattern.

The release was a minor with the changeset from the prerelease. After publishing I checked the package on npm and installed it in a clean folder to see that the types resolve. They did. The issue was closed with a link to the release.

summary: Planned support for reading a retry decision from provider error bodies after two users asked for it, and decided on a narrow hook instead of built in parsing for each provider.
body:
Two users asked in separate issues for the library to understand provider specific error bodies. One uses a provider that returns status 200 with an error object inside the body when it is overloaded, the other has a provider that sends a 400 with a message that actually means a temporary capacity problem.

My first thought was to add parsing for these providers. I looked at what that would take: each provider has its own shape, they change without notice, and I cannot test against real providers in CI because the tests use mocked models. A built in list would be wrong a few weeks after it was written.

The library already has a retryable function option that gets the error. The gap is that for the 200 case there is no error at all, since the call succeeds from the point of view of the AI SDK. That one is a different kind of problem, and it belongs to the bad response retries that already exist, where a result can be checked and rejected.

So I looked at the result check option. It exists, and it gets the result of generate. I verified with a test that a 200 with an error object in the content can be rejected by it and then retried. This means the first user needs no change in the library, only docs.

For the second user, the retryable function gets the APICallError, which has responseBody as a string. A user can parse it there. This also needs no change, but the docs do not show it.

So the plan is documentation only. I will write a recipes page with two recipes, one for each case, using generic names instead of provider names so that they stay true. I will also add a type test that responseBody is accessible in the function argument, since the recipe depends on it.

I replied to both users with the plan and the two snippets. One of them already confirmed that the snippet works on their side. The other asked whether the result check also runs for streams, and I said no, and that I need to check what the docs say on this. That check comes next.

summary: Wrote the recipes page for provider specific errors with two examples and added a type test that responseBody is readable in the retryable function.
body:
I wrote the recipes page I planned last time. It has two recipes: one that rejects a successful response whose content is an error object, and one that reads responseBody in the retryable function to detect a temporary capacity message.

Each recipe is short, with the code, one sentence on when to use it and one on the limits. The first one states clearly that the result check works for generate and not for streams, because a stream result is only known after the stream is read.

The second recipe uses JSON.parse inside a try block, since the body might not be JSON, and the docs example shows that case so nobody gets a thrown parse error inside the retry loop. I tested that case: a thrown error inside the retryable function currently propagates out of the loop. That is surprising enough that I want to think about whether the library should catch it.

The type test passes: responseBody is typed as a string or undefined on APICallError and the function argument is the generic error type. I had to narrow with an instanceof check, which the recipe now shows.

I added the page to the docs navigation and linked it from the options reference. The thrown error question I put in a new issue as a note for later.

summary: Decided that an exception thrown inside a user's retryable function is passed on as the original error with a logged note, and implemented it with tests for generate and stream.
body:
Last time I found that an exception thrown by the user's retryable function propagates out of the loop in a confusing way. Today I worked out what should happen and did it.

The options I considered were three. First, let it propagate as it does. The user sees their own exception and the original model error is lost, which makes debugging hard. Second, catch it and treat the error as non retryable. That hides a bug in the user's function and quietly turns off retries. Third, catch it, treat the error as not retryable, throw the original model error, and report the exception through the logging hook.

I chose the third. The caller gets the error they would have gotten without retries, which is the least surprising result, and the failure of the function is visible in the logs. A broken check should not make a working call fail with a different error.

The implementation wraps the call to the function in a try block in one place, the helper that decides on retryability. Since both generate and stream call this helper, the change is in one spot. The hook gets a new event name, retryable-check-failed, with the thrown value attached. I followed the naming of the other events.

The tests cover a function that throws a plain Error, one that throws a string, and one that returns a rejected promise, since the function may be async. The async case needed an await in the helper that was missing, which I found only because of that test. It passed after I added the await.

I also checked the circuit breaker: the failure is not counted, since the error is treated as non retryable. That matches the rule from before.

The docs got a short paragraph in the options reference and a line in the recipes page. The changeset is a patch. I did not release yet, because I want to look at one more issue first, and the evening is nearly over.

summary: Released the patch for exceptions in the retryable function together with a docs fix, after checking the logging event name against the existing ones.
body:
I read the event names of the logging hook once more before releasing, to be sure the new one fits. They are retry, fallback, giving-up, breaker-open and breaker-close. The new one, retryable-check-failed, is longer but says what happened, and I decided to keep it.

One issue came up in the type of the event. The union of events is exported, and adding a member can break a user's exhaustive switch. That sounds like a breaking change. I looked at it and concluded that adding events to a logging union is normal for a minor, but this is a patch. So I changed the changeset to a minor and wrote the note about the new event at the top.

I ran the whole test suite, the type tests and the build. All passed. I also grepped the docs for the list of events and found that the breaker events were missing from it, so I added them in the same commit.

Then I released. After release I installed the package in the sandbox project and triggered the new event with a throwing function to see the log line. It printed the event name and the thrown value as intended.

summary: A user reported that backoff delays ignored the Retry-After header when it was given in seconds with a decimal, and I reproduced the parse failure.
body:
The report said that a provider sends 'Retry-After: 1.5' and the library waited its normal backoff instead of one and a half seconds. The header spec says whole seconds, but this provider sends decimals anyway.

I looked at the parser from the Retry-After work months ago. It used a regular expression for digits only and then tried a date parse, which fails for '1.5', so the header was ignored and the fallback to the normal delay applied.

I wrote a test with the value '1.5' and expected a delay of 1500 milliseconds. It failed as the user said. I also wrote tests for '0.5', '2.', and '.5', and for a negative value, which must be ignored.

I decided to accept decimals, because being lenient with a header value that is clearly a number is harmless. The maxRetryAfter cap still applies after parsing, so a huge decimal cannot cause a long wait.

I changed the parser to use Number on a trimmed string that matches a plain number pattern, and kept the date path for everything else. All the new tests pass and the old ones too. Next is the changeset and a patch release, and a reply to the user.

summary: Released the decimal Retry-After fix as a patch and replied to the reporter with the version number.
body:
I wrote the changeset for the decimal Retry-After parsing as a patch. The text says that decimal seconds are now accepted and that negative values are still ignored.

Before releasing I ran the type tests and the build. I also tried the example from the issue in the sandbox project with a mocked response that has the header '1.5'. The log showed a delay of 1500 milliseconds.

The release went out in a few minutes. I replied to the reporter with the version and asked them to say if their provider sends any other odd forms. They answered a little later that decimals were the only case. I closed the issue.

summary: Looked into why the test suite became slow after the last releases and found that fake timers were left running in the circuit breaker tests, then fixed the setup.
body:
The CI run time had grown from about twenty seconds to over a minute, and I wanted to know why before it got worse. I ran Vitest locally with the reporter that shows the duration of each file.

One file stood out: the circuit breaker integration tests took forty seconds. Everything else was normal. I opened it and found tests that use real timers with a short cooldown of a few hundred milliseconds, while other tests in the same file use fake timers. The two styles were mixed, and a few tests waited in real time.

I first thought the cooldown tests were the problem, but after counting, they only explained about five seconds. The rest came from a beforeEach that created a new mocked model with a delay of two seconds and never cleared it. With fake timers off, each test waited for that delay.

I changed the file to use fake timers everywhere with vi.useFakeTimers in the setup and vi.useRealTimers in the cleanup, and replaced the real waits with advanceTimersByTimeAsync. The mocked delay now advances with the clock.

The file takes under a second now, and the whole suite is back at about eighteen seconds. I ran the suite five times to check that nothing became flaky, because async timer advancing can hide ordering problems. All runs passed.

I also looked for the same pattern elsewhere and found one more test with a real wait of one second in the stream tests. I changed that as well. I added a note to the contributing file about using fake timers for anything with a delay, since a contributor could easily repeat the mistake. No release is needed for this, since only tests changed.

summary: Started adding a timeout per attempt option after a request, wrote the design and the first implementation on top of the abort signal logic, with two open questions left.
body:
A user asked for a timeout per attempt: if one call to a model takes longer than a limit, cancel it and retry or fall back, instead of waiting for the provider to answer. Today they have to build it with an abort signal outside the library, and that cancels the whole operation, not one attempt.

I think this is a good fit for the library, since a hanging call is one of the failures it should handle. The abort handling from earlier work already creates a signal per attempt that links to the caller's signal. So the base exists.

The design is an option called attemptTimeout in milliseconds. For each attempt the loop creates a timer, and when it fires, it aborts the attempt signal with a TimeoutError, which is classified as retryable. The caller's own abort still wins and is never retried. The timer is cleared when the attempt finishes.

I wrote the first implementation in the attempt step. For generate it wraps the call, for stream it applies until the first chunk arrives, and after that the timer is cleared, matching the rule that a stream is only retried before the first chunk. I think that is the right meaning, and I will say it in the docs.

The tests use fake timers and a mocked model that never resolves. The first test passes: the timeout fires, the second attempt succeeds. The second test is for the caller's abort during an attempt, and it checks that the error is the abort error and not the timeout. It passes too.

Two questions are open. The first is the name of the error: AI SDK has its own timeout handling in newer versions, and I need to see whether it throws something I should recognize. The second is whether the timeout should count in the circuit breaker. My view is yes, since a hanging model is unhealthy, but I want a test and a sentence in the docs.

I did not write the docs yet. I stopped here because the evening was getting late and the open questions need a clear head. The branch of work is uncommitted, so I made a commit with a message that says work in progress.

summary: Answered the two open questions on the attempt timeout: it uses the library's own TimeoutError and counts toward the circuit breaker, with a test for each.
body:
I looked at the AI SDK for how it signals a timeout in the version I support. It aborts with a DOMException named TimeoutError when its own timeout setting is used, so a name check on the error is enough to recognize it in both cases.

I made the library throw an error with the same name and the same class family when its attempt timeout fires, so the existing classification treats both the same. A user who catches TimeoutError by name gets the same behavior from either source.

For the circuit breaker I wrote a test where three timeouts in a row open the breaker, and it passes with no code change, because the error is retryable and the breaker counts retryable errors. I wrote one sentence about this for the docs.

The remaining work is the docs and a stream test for the case where the first chunk arrives just before the timeout. I will do these next.

summary: Finished the attempt timeout with the stream edge case, the docs and a minor release, and noted that the option applies per attempt and not to the whole operation.
body:
The attempt timeout is done. The stream test I still needed covers a first chunk that arrives right before the timer fires. With fake timers I advanced to one millisecond before the limit, emitted the chunk, and then advanced past the limit. The stream stayed open and the timer did not abort it, as intended.

I found one bug while writing it. The timer was cleared when the first chunk was read, but if the consumer did not read the stream right away, the timer could fire before the first read. The first chunk is what matters, not the first read, so I moved the clearing to the point where the model's own stream produces the chunk. The test now passes.

The docs got a section with the option, a short example with a fallback list, and three notes: it applies to each attempt, not to the whole operation; for streams it ends at the first chunk; and it counts toward the circuit breaker. I also added a sentence that a total limit is still done with an abort signal from outside.

The type for the option allows a number, and I added it to the per model override as well, so a slow model can have a longer limit. The type tests cover both positions.

I ran everything and published a prerelease first, then asked the requester to try it. Their reply came within the hour. It worked on their slow provider, and they used the per model override for one model. I released it as a minor and closed the issue.

summary: Reviewed the dependency updates for the AI SDK peer range and the test tooling, and confirmed that nothing breaks with the newest SDK minor.
body:
The automatic update pull requests had piled up for two weeks, so I went through them in one session. There were five: the newest AI SDK minor as a dev dependency, Vitest, tsdown, the changesets package and a GitHub Actions version.

I started with the SDK, because the library depends on its types. I ran the full tests and the type tests against it. Everything passed, but I looked at the changelog of the SDK for anything about errors, since the retry logic depends on the error classes. There was one new field on APICallError, and nothing was removed.

I also ran the tests against the lowest supported SDK version, using the matrix job in the workflow. It passed too, so the peer range stays as it is.

Vitest had a minor update that changed the default for fake timers: the faked functions list now includes one more entry. My tests that use fake timers passed anyway. I merged it.

For tsdown, I compared the output files before and after with a diff of the dist folder. The only difference was the order of two exports in the declaration file.
