That is harmless, but I checked that the package exports map still resolves for both module formats by running the check script. It did.

Changesets and the Actions version were simple. I merged all five after the green runs. No release was needed, since only dev dependencies changed. I noted in the journal that the matrix job proved its worth here, and I will keep it.

summary: Debugged a report of doubled delays when both the Retry-After header and the exponential backoff apply, and found the delay was added instead of replaced.
body:
A user wrote that their calls waited about twice as long as the header said. A provider sent 'Retry-After: 10' and the log showed a delay of around 21 seconds before the next attempt.

I first suspected the decimal parsing from earlier, but the value was a plain 10. So I looked at how the delay is calculated. The loop computes the backoff delay with jitter, then reads the header, and the rule is that the larger of the two wins. That is what the docs say.

I reproduced it with a mocked error that has the header and a backoff base of 10 seconds. The result was 20 seconds plus jitter. So this user simply had a large backoff base, and the larger value won as documented. It was not a bug in the delay math.

But it raised a fair point. The user expected that the header replaces the backoff, since the server told them exactly how long to wait. With the max rule, a big backoff base makes the library wait longer than the server asked. I looked at what the header means: the server says the earliest time to retry, so waiting longer is allowed, only waiting less is wrong. The current rule is safe.

Still, I want to make the user's case possible. An option like retryAfterMode with 'max' as the default and 'exact' as the alternative would do it, but I hesitate to add an option for one report. The user can already pass a function as the backoff that reads the error and returns the header value, since the backoff accepts a function of the error and the attempt.

I tested that: a backoff function that returns the parsed header in milliseconds works, but it needs the parsing, and the parser is internal. I exported nothing yet. Exporting the parser as a helper is small and useful, so I will think about it.

I replied to the user with the explanation, the function recipe, and a promise to decide on the helper soon. I did not change the code. I wrote down in the issue that the default is max by design.

summary: Exported the Retry-After parser as a small helper with its own tests and wrote a recipe for using the exact server delay, instead of adding a new option.
body:
After last time's report about doubled delays I decided on the helper, not an option. The helper is called parseRetryAfter, takes the error or the response headers, and returns the delay in milliseconds or undefined.

The reasoning is that an option for the mode adds one more thing to explain in the docs, the types and the per model overrides, for a need that a short function covers. A helper adds one export and removes the need to copy the parsing code.

The parser already existed inside the library, so the work was mostly in the surface. I moved it to its own file, gave it a signature that accepts an APICallError, a headers object or a Headers instance, and exported it from the package entry. The decimal and date cases from earlier work are still handled, and the maxRetryAfter cap is not applied inside it, since the cap belongs to the loop and the helper should return what the server said.

I wrote tests for each input form and for the missing header. I also added a type test that the return type is number or undefined.

The recipe for the docs shows a backoff function that calls the helper and falls back to a fixed delay when it returns undefined. I ran this recipe as a real test too, with a mocked error, to make sure the snippet in the docs works, and it gave exactly 10000 milliseconds for a header of 10.

I noticed one problem while doing this. The backoff function receives the error, but for a Headers instance the header name is case insensitive and for a plain object it is not. My helper lowercases the keys of a plain object before reading. A test covers 'retry-after' and 'Retry-After' in a plain object.

The changeset is a minor, since there is a new export. I published a prerelease and asked the reporter to try the recipe, then released after they said it worked. I closed the issue with a link to the recipe.

summary: Triaged a quiet stretch of issues: one stale question closed, one request for a metrics hook that I turned into a docs example of the logging hook, and one duplicate.
body:
There were three open issues after a quiet couple of weeks, so I went through them.

The first was a question from a month ago about passing different options to generate and stream. The reporter never answered my last reply, which had the recipe with two wrappers, so I closed it with a friendly note that they can reopen it.

The second was a request for a metrics hook, to count retries and fallbacks in a monitoring system. I looked at the logging hooks and saw that the events already contain everything needed: the event name, the model id, the attempt number, the error and the delay. A separate metrics hook would duplicate that.

Instead I wrote a docs example that turns the logging hook into counters. It uses a plain object as the counter store and shows how to label by model id and event name. It is generic and does not name a monitoring product, so it stays true when those tools change. I tested the example in the sandbox project with a mocked failing model and the counters came out right: three retry events and one fallback event for a scripted run.

The third issue was a duplicate of the decimal Retry-After report from before, from a user on an older version. I answered with the version that fixed it and closed it as a duplicate.

I also looked at the download numbers and the open pull requests, and there are none waiting. The docs example went into the next docs deploy. I did not write a changeset, since the library itself did not change. Next I will look at whether the README still shows the best first example, because the options have grown since it was written.

summary: Started on a request for a per-model retry budget after a user wrote that fallback chains retry too long, and sketched two designs without picking one yet.
body:
A user opened an issue saying that with three models in a fallback chain, a bad outage meant every model burned its full maxAttempts before the call failed. Their calls took over a minute. I reproduced it with mocked providers that always return a 503, and counted the attempts: with maxAttempts 4 and three models the loop made 12 calls.

I sketched two designs. The first is a total budget for the whole operation, counted across models. The second is a per-model limit that is smaller for fallback models than for the first one. The total budget is simpler to explain, but it can starve the last model of any attempt when the first model is flaky.

I wrote both as short pseudo-code in a scratch file and checked where each would touch the attempt loop. The total budget needs a counter that lives outside the per-model state, which is not there today. The per-model limit fits the existing options shape better, since models can already carry their own options.

I also thought about how this interacts with the attempt timeout released a while ago. That option is per attempt, so neither design changes it, but the docs must say clearly that the new budget counts attempts and not time.

I did not pick a design. I asked the reporter what they need: a cap on total calls or a cap on total time. Their answer decides whether this is an attempt budget at all or just a deadline for the whole operation, which would be a different feature built on the abort signal.

Next step is to wait for the reply, then write the design in the issue so that others can comment before I touch the code.

summary: The reporter wants a deadline for the whole operation, not an attempt count, so I dropped the budget idea and wrote the design for a total timeout built on the abort signal.
body:
The reporter answered within the hour: what they care about is that the user waits no longer than about twenty seconds, whatever the number of attempts. That makes it a deadline, and an attempt budget would only approximate it badly because delays vary with backoff and Retry-After.

I wrote the design in the issue. A new option, totalTimeout, creates an internal abort signal that fires after the given time and is combined with the user's own signal. When it fires, the loop stops, including during a backoff sleep, and throws the library's TimeoutError with a message that says it was the total deadline.

Two details needed a decision. First, if an attempt is running when the deadline hits, it is aborted, and the error from that attempt is not retried. Second, a backoff delay that would end after the deadline should not be slept at all, because waiting and then failing is worse than failing early. I chose to fail early with the last real error attached as the cause.

I checked the existing abort code in src/abort.ts and found that combining signals is already done for the attempt timeout, so most of the work is reuse. I did not start the implementation. I listed the tests to write: deadline during an attempt, deadline during a sleep, a delay longer than the remaining time, and the user signal winning over the deadline.

The reporter thumbs-upped the design. Implementation starts next session.

summary: Implemented the totalTimeout option on the abort signal logic, including early failure when the next backoff delay would pass the deadline, with six tests.
body:
I implemented totalTimeout as designed in the issue. The loop now creates a deadline signal at the start and combines it with the user signal through the helper that the attempt timeout already uses. Each attempt gets the combined signal, and the backoff sleep listens to it too.

The early failure was the fiddly part. Before sleeping, the loop computes the remaining time. If the delay is larger than what is left, it throws a TimeoutError with the last attempt error as the cause, without sleeping. I first compared against the delay alone, then noticed that the Retry-After value can raise the delay after jitter, so the check now uses the final delay.

Tests, all with fake timers:
- the deadline fires during an attempt and the attempt is aborted
- the deadline fires during a sleep
- a delay longer than the remaining time fails at once
- the user signal aborts first and the error is the user's abort, not a timeout
- no deadline set, behavior unchanged
- a fallback to a second model still respects the same deadline

The last test caught a bug: I had created the deadline signal inside the per-model function, so each model got a fresh deadline. Moving it to the top of the operation fixed it.

Streams work the same way before the first chunk. After the first chunk the deadline does not abort the stream, because the retry logic is already out of the picture then, and I wrote that into a code comment. I am not sure this is what users expect, so I will raise it in the docs and ask the reporter.

The full suite passes and the types check. Docs and the changeset are still open.

summary: Wrote the docs section and the changeset for totalTimeout, stating that it covers attempts and sleeps but not a stream after its first chunk.
body:
I added a section to the options page for totalTimeout with a short example that combines it with maxAttempts and a fallback model. It says in plain words that the deadline covers all attempts, all backoff sleeps and all models in the chain.

I added a note about streams: once the first chunk has been delivered, the deadline no longer applies, because the library does not control the stream after that point. I also linked the section on the per-attempt timeout and put a small table next to it that shows which option limits what.

The changeset is a minor bump with two sentences. I asked the reporter in the issue to try a prerelease and to say whether the stream behavior surprises them.

summary: The reporter tried the prerelease of totalTimeout and was fine with the stream behavior, so I released it as a minor and closed the issue with the version number.
body:
The reporter installed the prerelease the evening before and ran it against their real fallback chain during a provider slowdown. Their calls now fail after about twenty seconds with the TimeoutError, where before they ran past a minute.

On streams they wrote that a deadline after the first chunk would be wrong for them anyway, since long answers are normal. So the documented behavior stays.

Before releasing I ran the full suite once more and built with tsdown to check that the type exports include the new option in both the ESM and CJS declarations. They do. I merged the changeset pull request that the release action had opened and watched the publish job finish.

I replied in the issue with the version number and closed it. I also added a line to the pinned discussion, since a few people there had asked about long waits in fallback chains.

summary: Debugged a report that onRetry received the wrong attempt number after a fallback to the second model, and found the counter was reset per model while the docs said it was global.
body:
A user logging with onRetry noticed that after the first model failed, the attempt number in the event went back to one. They expected it to keep counting across models, as the docs sentence on the event says.

I wrote a test with two mocked models that both fail twice and print the attempt numbers: 1, 2, then 1, 2. That confirmed the report. The counter lives in the per-model function, and the event gets that local value.

The question was which side is wrong, the docs or the code. Two things argued for changing the docs: the per-model count is what maxAttempts limits, and changing the number would alter what existing users see in their logs. So I kept the numbers and decided to add a second field instead. The event now has attempt, which is per model, and totalAttempts, which counts across the chain. That is additive and not a breaking change.

I implemented the field, updated the event type, and extended the test to check both values. I rewrote the docs sentence so it states what attempt means, and added totalAttempts to the event table.

I also checked the logging hook event for streams and the circuit breaker events, and the new field is only on the retry events, where it makes sense.

The patch is not released yet. I will bundle it with the next small fix.

summary: Reviewed a pull request that adds a Vitest helper for mocking failing models, and asked to move it out of the public exports before merging.
body:
A contributor sent a pull request with a helper, createFailingModel, that makes tests of the library's users easier. The code is clean and has tests of its own.

My concern was the place. The helper was exported from the package entry, which makes it part of the public API and ties it to Vitest conventions. People using Jest would get an export they cannot really use, and I would have to keep it stable.

I suggested two ways: a separate entry point, ai-retry/testing, or no export and a docs recipe with the code to copy. I leaned toward the recipe, because the helper is only about thirty lines and the AI SDK already ships mock models that most users would build on.

I also pointed out two small things in the diff. The helper swallowed the error type and always threw APICallError, and the test file used a hard-coded delay instead of fake timers.

The contributor replied that the recipe is fine with them. I said I would merge once the export is removed and the code moved into the docs page. No code from the pull request will be in the package itself.

summary: Released the totalAttempts patch together with the testing recipe from the contributor's pull request, after checking that the changeset text matches what changed.
body:
The contributor moved the helper into a docs recipe and fixed the fake timers in the example. I read the recipe once more by running its code in a scratch test against the current build, and it worked without changes.

I merged the pull request and added a changeset for the totalAttempts field as a patch. I thought about calling it a minor because it adds a field, but the event type is only read by users, so it does not break anyone, and the project has treated additions to event payloads as patches before.

The release action opened its version pull request. I looked at the generated changelog and found that the recipe commit was listed as a change of the package, which it is not, so I edited the changeset to leave docs-only changes out.

After publishing I installed the new version in a clean directory, ran a three-line script that triggers a fallback, and checked that the event printed both attempt and totalAttempts. It did.

I answered the original reporter with the version and a short explanation of why the existing field kept its meaning. They said the new field is exactly what they needed for their dashboard.

summary: Investigated why a fallback model with a different provider options object lost its options, and found the options were merged from the first model instead of replaced.
body:
A user configured two models with different providerOptions, one for each provider. When the fallback ran, the second provider rejected a field that belonged to the first one. That sounded like a merge instead of a replacement.

I reproduced it with two mocked models that record the options they receive. The second model got the union of both option sets. The cause was in the attempt step, where the options for a fallback were built with a spread over the options of the previous attempt, so keys from the first model stayed in.

The fix is to build the options for each model from the original call options plus that model's own overrides, never from the previous attempt. I changed the function that prepares the attempt and removed the object that carried state between models.

Then I wrote three tests: no leak of keys from model one into model two, overrides of model two win over the call options, and a retry on the same model keeps the same options. The first one failed before the change and passes now.

I looked for other state that crosses models. The headers had the same pattern, so I fixed that too and added a test. The abort signal is shared on purpose.

This fix changes behavior that someone might have relied on, though I think it is unlikely. I will release it as a patch and mention the change clearly in the changeset. Docs for the option precedence were thin, so I added a short paragraph with the order: call options, then model options.

The release will wait for one more day in case the reporter wants to test.

summary: The reporter confirmed the provider options fix with a prerelease, and I released it as a patch with a clear note about the changed behavior.
body:
The reporter ran the prerelease against both of their providers and wrote that the rejected field is gone and the fallback now works. They also asked whether a way exists to share options between models on purpose. The answer is yes: call-level options apply to every model, and model-level options only to that model.

Before the release I went through the issues for anything that might have depended on the leak. I found none open, and I searched the closed ones for providerOptions and found two old threads, both about the options being ignored, not merged.

I wrote the changeset as a patch with this text: options for a fallback model are now built from the call options and its own overrides, and no longer inherit keys from a failed model. I thought about a minor, since behavior changes, but the old behavior was a bug and the docs never promised it.

The release action ran green. I installed the published version in a clean project and used the reporter's two-provider setup with mock models to check the option objects once more.

I also updated the precedence paragraph in the docs with an example that shows both levels, because the reporter's question showed that the text was not clear enough.

Then I looked at the open issue list. Four are open: one feature request for a metrics hook that already has a docs example, one question about edge runtime, one about Bun, and one about the type of the retryable function. I replied to the edge runtime question by pointing at the network error support and asked for their runtime and error output.

Nothing else is planned for this morning. The Bun question needs a reproduction.

summary: Reproduced the Bun report: the library works, but a TypeError message differs there, so the network error detection missed one connection reset shape.
body:
The user on Bun said that dropped connections were not retried. I set up Bun in a scratch directory with a local server that closes the socket mid-response and called a mocked fetch-backed model through the library.

The error that came out was a TypeError with the message "The socket connection was closed unexpectedly" and no cause. The detection I wrote some weeks ago looks at the error code in the cause or at a list of message fragments from Node and browsers. Bun's message matched none of them.

I added the fragment to the list and a test with an error object of that shape. I also reviewed the whole list, since it is only a list of strings, and moved it into a named constant with a comment on which runtime each entry comes from, so that the next report is easier to place.

I did not want to match every TypeError, because programming errors would then be retried, and that was the reason for the list in the first place. I kept it narrow.

I asked the user to try a prerelease against their real setup, since my local server is only one of several ways to drop a connection.

The suite passes on Node. I do not run the tests on Bun in CI and I wondered whether I should. It would cost a job and some minutes, and there is only one report so far, so I decided against it for now.

summary: The Bun user confirmed the prerelease, and I released the connection reset fix as a patch and added the runtimes list to the docs page on network errors.
body:
The user ran the prerelease in their Bun service and wrote that the dropped connections are now retried and the logging hook shows the attempts.

I released the fix as a patch. The changeset says that one more connection error message from Bun is recognized.

In the docs page on retried network errors I added a short section that says which runtimes were checked: Node, browsers through the SDK and Bun. It also says how to extend the detection through the retryable function, with a three-line example, for runtimes with other messages. That seemed better than promising coverage that I cannot test.

The release job passed and I checked the published package contents with npm pack to make sure that only the dist folder and the readme are in it.

I answered the edge runtime question too: the reporter had replied with their error, which was a plain AbortError from the platform's own request limit. That is not something the library should retry, as the abort handling treats it as a stop. I explained this and linked the docs on abort signals, and they said that makes sense.

That leaves two open issues, the metrics hook and the retryable type.

summary: Looked into the open issue on the type of the retryable function and found that the error argument is typed as unknown, which forces casts for the common APICallError case.
body:
The issue says that writing a custom retryable function needs a cast every time: the error argument is unknown, so reading statusCode or responseBody means checking the type first. The reporter suggests typing it as APICallError.

That would be wrong, since the function also receives network TypeErrors, timeouts and anything the model throws. Typing it as APICallError would make the type lie and hide the check that users need.

So I looked for a better option than a cast. The library already exports an isAPICallError guard because the SDK has one. I checked that the docs mention it, and they do, but only on the errors page, not in the retryable examples. The recipes page uses it, but the main options page shows a cast.

I considered three changes:
- type the argument as a union of known error types and unknown
- add a small helper, getStatusCode(error), that returns a number or undefined
- only fix the docs

The union with unknown collapses to unknown in TypeScript, so it would not help. The helper hides the guard and adds API that is easy to get wrong. The docs fix costs nothing and solves the actual complaint, which is that the example is bad.

I rewrote the example on the options page to use the guard from the SDK, and replaced the cast. I also added a type test that checks that inside the guard branch the statusCode property is readable without a cast, so a future change to the types cannot break the example silently.

I wrote a reply to the reporter that explains why the argument stays unknown and shows the guard version of their code. I did not close the issue and waited for them to say whether the example solves it.

While in the file I noticed that the onRetry docs also had a cast, and fixed that too. The suite and the docs build pass. This is only docs and a type test, so there is no release.

summary: The retryable type reporter accepted the guard example, so I closed the issue, and spent the rest of the morning reviewing the README for statements that are out of date.
body:
The reporter replied that the guard version of their function is fine and a little clearer than the cast, so I closed the issue with a link to the changed docs section.

With a quiet morning I read the README from top to bottom against the current behavior. It is the first thing users see, and several releases have passed since I last read it as a whole.

I found four problems. The feature list did not mention the total timeout or the network errors. The example with the fallback used an option name that is deprecated in the major release and that now throws a ConfigError. One sentence said that streams are never retried, which is only true after the first chunk. The badge for the supported SDK range showed the older range.

I fixed all four. For the stream sentence I used the wording from the docs page, so the two places say the same thing.

I ran every code block of the README through the type checker by pasting them into a scratch file, and found that one example was missing an import. I added it.

I think this check should be a test: extract the code blocks and compile them. I wrote the idea into the notes file for later, because the extraction script has details like blocks that are meant as fragments.

The change is docs only and will go out with the next release.

summary: Built a small script that compiles the TypeScript code blocks of the README and docs in CI, and it immediately found two broken examples in the docs.
body:
I took up the idea from the morning. The script reads the markdown files, extracts blocks tagged ts, writes each to a temporary file and runs the TypeScript compiler on all of them with the library path mapped to the source.

Fragments were the first problem. Some blocks show only a call without imports or setup. I decided on a marker: a block whose info string says ts fragment is skipped. That keeps the check honest and makes it visible in the markdown which examples are partial.

The first run failed on eleven blocks. Nine were fragments that I marked. Two were real errors in the docs: one used the removed positional onRetry signature from before the major release, and one passed a string as a fallback, which is now a ConfigError. Both had survived the migration, because I had edited the guide and not the recipes.

I fixed both blocks to use the current object forms. The run then passed, in about six seconds on my machine.

I added the script as an npm script, check:docs, and as a step in the CI workflow after the type check. I made it run only when markdown or source files change, to avoid wasting time, but then realized that the path filter on the workflow also applies to other jobs, so I put the condition on the step instead.

I pushed to a test pull request to see the workflow run. The step passed, and when I added a deliberately wrong example, it failed with a readable message that names the file and the line of the block. I removed the example.

There is one limitation: the script checks that examples compile, not that they behave correctly. I think that is enough for now.

summary: Released a patch with the README fixes and the Bun note, and wrote the contributing notes about the docs check so that pull requests with examples do not fail without explanation.
body:
With the docs check in place, I added a short section to CONTRIBUTING.md. It says that code blocks in markdown are compiled in CI, that partial examples need the fragment marker, and how to run the check locally with one command.

I also added the check to the pull request template as a checkbox, though I know people rarely read it. The error message of the script mentions the marker, which probably helps more than the template.

Then I prepared the release. Since the last one only docs changed, but the package readme is part of the npm page, a patch release makes the corrected README visible there. I wrote a changeset that says so in one sentence, and the release action published it.

After the release I opened the npm page and checked the readme: the fallback example and the badge are right now. The old sentence about streams is gone.

I looked at the open issues again. Only the metrics hook request is open, with the docs example added earlier. The requester has not answered in three weeks, so I commented that I will close it in a week if there is no reply, and left it open.

I wrote down in the notes what is likely next: the circuit breaker has no documented way to reset its state in tests, and two users asked indirectly through the example code. I will look at that when I get to it.

summary: Looked at how users reset circuit breaker state between tests, found that it is shared per model id across calls, and designed an explicit reset function instead of changing the sharing.
body:
A user asked in a discussion how to keep tests independent, because after one test fails a mocked model several times, the circuit breaker opens and the next test fails right away with the circuit open error. That is a fair complaint about test isolation.

I reproduced it with two tests in one file using the same mock model id. The second test failed with the circuit open error, as the user said. The state is kept in a module-level map keyed by model id, which is deliberate: in a server, the breaker has to be shared across requests, or it would never open.

I considered three solutions. A per-instance breaker would break the sharing that makes it useful. A reset on the options object would let users reset the state of a single call, but not between tests. An exported resetCircuitBreakers function is blunt and works for tests.

I chose the exported function, with an optional model id argument so that a single model can be reset. It clears the map, or deletes one key. I named it resetCircuitBreakers and documented it as meant for tests.

I also thought about letting users pass their own store object, which would make it possible to keep state in Redis for several server instances. That is a much larger feature, and nobody asked for it. I noted it in the design comment as a possible direction and left it out.

The implementation took a few lines. The tests: after opening the breaker, the call fails fast, and after the reset, the call goes through again. A second test checks that resetting one id leaves another one open.

I wrote the docs section on the circuit breaker page, with a Vitest example using beforeEach. The README and docs check passed on the new code block.

I also noticed that my own test suite relied on unique model ids to avoid the same problem. I changed it to call the reset in a global setup file, which makes the tests less fragile.

The change is a minor release, since it adds an export. I will publish it after replying to the discussion and letting the user try a prerelease.

summary: The discussion user confirmed that resetCircuitBreakers fixes their test isolation, so I released it as a minor and linked the docs section in the reply.
body:
The user tried the prerelease in their test suite and wrote that the beforeEach reset makes their tests independent. They also asked whether the function should be called automatically by the test framework. I said no, since the library has no way to know about the framework and a hidden hook would surprise people.

I merged the version pull request and the release job published the minor. I installed it into a scratch project and called the function with and without an id, and both worked as documented.

The changeset text says the function was added for test isolation and that production code should not call it. I repeated that in the docs, because a reset in production would silently close a breaker that is protecting a failing provider.

I replied in the discussion with the version and the link. I also went through the circuit breaker page once more and added the reset function to the list of exports at its top.

summary: A user reported that the logging hook receives the raw error object including headers with an API key, so I checked what the library passes to hooks and what it should redact.
body:
The report said that the onRetry event contains the error, and the APICallError from the SDK carries requestBodyValues and responseHeaders. When the user logged the event to a third-party service, an authorization header showed up in the logs.

I checked the error object in a test with a mocked 429 response. The SDK error includes the response headers and the request body values, but the request headers are not part of it in the version I tested. The user used a custom fetch that attached the key to the error itself, which is outside the library.

Still, the report points to something real: the library passes the original error to the hooks, and users tend to log whole events. I thought about redacting in the library, but the error is the user's data and changing it would also break the instanceof checks that users do in their hooks.

So I decided against modifying the error. The better answer is a docs warning that the event holds the original error, which can contain whatever the SDK or a custom fetch puts on it, and a recipe for logging only selected fields: status code, attempt, delay and the error message.

I wrote the recipe with a small function, toLogEntry, that picks those fields, and put the warning next to the event table. The docs check compiled the example.

I replied to the reporter with this reasoning and asked if the recipe fits their case. I also asked them to check the custom fetch for where the key gets attached to the error.

No code change, so no release.

summary: The reporter found the key came from their own fetch wrapper and thanked me for the logging recipe, so I closed the issue and added a line about it to the docs warning.
body:
The reporter replied that their custom fetch added the authorization header to a property on the thrown error for debugging, and that this was the source. They removed it and will use the recipe for their log entries.

I closed the issue. Before that I added one sentence to the docs warning: errors thrown by custom fetch functions are passed on as they are, with all their properties. That was the missing piece in my first text, which only mentioned the SDK.

I also searched the library source for other places where the error object is attached to events, to make sure the stream path and the circuit breaker events behave the same. They pass the original error as well, so the warning applies to all of them.

I checked the docs build and the docs check, both passed. The change is in the next release, since it is only text.

I looked at the metrics hook issue, which had no answer, and the week was up. I closed it with a comment that points at the logging hook example and that says it can be reopened with a concrete need.

summary: Planned the next minor release by listing the merged changes since the last one, and decided to hold it for a docs pass on the guides about fallbacks and timeouts.
body:
I went through the commits since the last published version to see what a release would contain. There are only docs changes: the logging warning, the recipe for log entries, the guard example for the retryable function and the README fixes that were already published.

So a release is not needed right now. A patch only for docs is possible, but I did one a few days ago and do not want to publish a version just for sentences. I decided to wait until there is a code change.

Instead I used the time on a docs pass that I had in mind for some time. The guides on fallbacks and timeouts were written at different times and use different words. The fallback guide says deadline in one place, total timeout in another, and the timeouts guide says attempt limit where the option is called attemptTimeout.

I made a list of terms and used them consistently: attempt timeout for the per-attempt option, total timeout for the deadline, attempt for one call to a model, and chain for the ordered list of models. I replaced the variants in four pages.

I also added a small diagram in text form to the timeouts guide that shows an operation with three attempts and a backoff sleep, and where each of the two timeouts applies. It was the thing the earlier issue reporters had trouble imagining.

The docs check passed. I read the pages once more in the built site and found a broken anchor link from the fallback guide, which I fixed.

For the next session, I have no open issue. I will look at the dependency updates when they arrive, and otherwise wait for reports.
